Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in the coordination of various industrial systems. The non-linearity and discreteness of such problems often make exact analytical solutions impossible, rendering them complex optimization challenges. To address these complexities, a novel multi-objective branch-and-bound algorithm has been developed, based on the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm version II (NSGA-II). The proposed algorithm combinatorially partitions the feasible region using branch cuts and eliminates non-optimal solutions by evaluating objective values at end-points. To optimize computational efficiency, NSGAII-guided exploratory sampling is employed, ultimately yielding a non-dominated solution set. We evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm through six test scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness with high quality solutions in all cases. To confirm convergence, an estimated solution set diameter is calculated for each test scenario, converging to zero as the algorithm terminates. The algorithm has been implemented in MATLAB and is publicly available at https://github.com/alirezaahmadi/multi-objective-MIP-solver. The results of our study demonstrate that NSGAII-guided branch-and-bound (NGSB) is a reliable and efficient algorithm for multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. Furthermore, through comparative analysis using six test scenarios involving multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), multi-objective linear programming (MLP), and multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming with additional non-linear constraints (MLP with N) problems, NGB consistently yields the most reliable solutions with the fewest interactions and the highest precision among various algorithms. To summate, NGB is an efficient and precise algorithm for multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming challenges. It is particularly suited for complex problems involving additional non-linear constraints, as validated by our experimental results. Moreover, to ensure the credibility of our study, detailed mathematical derivations and step-by-step examples for NGB have been provided. Consequently, the proposed algorithm is estimated to handle MO MIMO programming challenges effectively. It is noted, however, that NSGA-II has a relatively low population size due to the discrete variable part of the problem, and as a result, the proposed algorithm may experience performance degradation for problems involving a large number of integer variables, unless guided by more advanced techniques, for instance, density estimation approach. It is anticipated that the density evolutionary algorithm (DEA) can enhance the efficiency of NGB, and this expectation will be confirmed in our upcoming research on this particular variation of the algorithm. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. As a result, the experiment will boast an unparalleled dataset, featuring high-precision data on rare particles, as well as a thorough characterization of the underlying event. Furthermore, the addition of a completely new detector system will facilitate the simultaneous data collection of the event centrality and multiplicity classes, complete with the detection of electromagnetic radiation, charged particles, and also topological data. This cutting-edge upgrade will pave the way for the simultaneous observation of the underlying event in terms of both particle physics and detector response. Ultimately, the expanded capabilities of the ALICE experiment will equip the collaboration with a pioneering capability, allowing for the rigorous study of events characterized by low particle multiplicity and, as an added bonus, exceptional systematic reduction. As a result, the expanded ALICE capabilities will equip the experiment with a pioneering role in the study of the underlying event structure, while also marking one of the significant investments in the study of QCD as a social science. The Unruh effect suggests that a particle in a vacuum state emits entangled particles when accelerating, yet detecting it is challenging due to the lack of a stationary frame. We've found that the entanglement between forward and backward light cones in the Schwarzschild metric is a viable indicator of the Unruh effect, with a quantifiable value based on the Berry phase. This Berry phase can be calculated using a logarithmic Sobolev inequality, and it's also retrievable through a quantum clock interacting with a scalar field in a state influenced by the Unruh effect. This approach allows for the detection of the Unruh effect without a stationary frame, and it also implies the existence of a timelike Berry phase, which has theoretical and conceptual implications that need to be explored further. Using a timelike version of the geometric phase, the entanglement within the light cones can be calculated and potentially even observed experimentally in a setting of cosmological scale equivalence. Furthermore, the relationship between this timelike geometric phase and causality principles remains to be elucidated. The minimum amount of geometric phase (and hence entanglement within the light cones) that is achievable corresponds to the scenario in which an object is at rest, in which case the first derivative of the logarithm of the square root of the determinant of the metric's Jacobian is zero. This is an instance of a timelike geometric phase, and it is instrumental in establishing a lower bound for the entanglement within the light cones in the absence of acceleration. That is, even an accelerating observer can achieve a degree of nonlocality that is comparable to the scenario in which the object is at rest, and hence the unlocality inherent in the timelike geometric phase provides a universal lower bound for entanglement within the light cones in the non-accelerating case. That lower bound can be expressed as the Berry phase times $\hbar/2$ plus the logarithm of the square root of the determinant of the metric's Jacobian at rest. It is an open and interesting question whether a similar lower bound holds for the non-accelerating case in the accelerating scenario. That is, whether a degree of nonlocality that is inherent in the accelerating scenario can be achieved in the non-accelerating case. If so, what would be the relevant measure of nonlocality in the non-accelerating case and what would be the lower bound for nonlocality that is achievable at rest? These applications extend to various special bundles, such as tangent and cotangent bundles, holomorphic vector bundles of non-degenerate sections and Pfaffian bundles, exemplified in curves, surfaces and threefold varieties, which further enable derivation of invariants like Hilbert symbols and certain Fuchsian invariants, with an additional discussion on their relation to Euler characteristic and signatures of projective varieties. Last, the text presents methods for determining the global characteristics forms' degrees and pseudodegrees along with an examination of bundle monadics and the (co)boundaries with non-negative curvatures, with special consideration given to (co)Pfaffian forms and the Pfaffian boundary, derived in a formula, with an additional discussion on the degree of a non-regular global characteristics form, along with verification that a projective vector bundle of rank p has a global characteristics form of degree p when it is of non-degenerate sections. Moreover, the text investigates an algebraic approach to the problem of determining which vector bundles possess a global characteristics form and prove the existence, degree and vanishing degree of such a form for certain special vector bundles, with the final section encompassing some related results and problems. Anastasiadis and Kostantinidis introduced a novel theory to describe the mechanisms driving accretion flux variations in accreting compact objects, which Kostantinidis and Faehrmann later generalized for non-magnetized winds in black hole high-soft states. We developed a simplified version of their formula for the variable flux, which applies to the entire Stella/XRB code and specifically to Cyg X-1's corona in the hard state. We simulated this model in the Cyg X-1's high mass limit and observed its impact on X-ray variability. We discovered a correlation between variable flux and hard X-ray spectrum, which contributed 40% of the total variable flux in the 0.1-100 keV band, specifically affecting variability timescales ranging from milliseconds to minutes. These results support a multi-faceted nature to Cyg X-1's variable hard X-ray emission, specifically originating from the stellar breeze, disk-corona interface, and accretion disk. We further observed a distinct variable component in the millisecond range, likely stemming from these physical processes, which may explain the often-observed 0.1-10 kg s$^{-1}$ variable flux in the Stella code. We discovered two distinct variable components in the millisecond range for multi-component corona configurations and in the 10-60 s range for the stellar breeze, which may explain the often-observed power-law variability in the Stella code in these time ranges. We further developed a simplified version of the Stella code to specifically model the stellar breeze in Cyg X-1's hard state, which may explain several of its observed properties, potentially revealing the physical processes behind this phenomenon. Such a simplified version of the Stella code could help in the global modeling of Cyg X-1's accretion flow in its hard state, potentially revealing the physical processes behind its variable X-ray emission. These predicted variable components provide an opportunity to analyze and identify the stellar breeze in Cyg X-1's hard state, specifically ranging from 30 s to several hours, which can potentially be confirmed through the analysis of its future X-ray observations. These predicted variable components in the millisecond range for multi-component corona configurations may also be confirmed through the analysis of Cyg X-1's X-ray variability, which may also provide an empirical estimate of the multi-component corona's degree of freedom, potentially revealing the physical processes behind this phenomenon. Although both syntax and semantics are crucial components of natural language, most current models concentrate solely on capturing syntax. However, syntax ultimately serves to clarify meaning. In contrast, we suggest a unified approach that simultaneously determines both syntax and semantics. By jointly modeling universal syntax and meaning, this method can clarify the underlying role of syntax in clarifying meaning. Specifically, we suggest a universal meaning parser based on type logic that effectively translates natural language into a unified, machine-readable format. Subsequently, we present a neural network architecture capable of automatically learning this meaning representation from large-scale text data, accompanied by a corresponding syntax encoder to produce a universal syntax description. Empirical tests conducted on English and Chinese text demonstrate the feasibility and precision of this method in uncovering both syntax and semantics. Additionally, the learned syntax is shown to be applicable to various natural language tasks, including semantic parsing, syntax-dependent irregulair expression classification, and machine translation. We believe that presenting syntax and semantics in a unified manner offers a promising new direction for future natural language processing research. These "giant ECs" are early-type galaxies that exceed a certain size and are characterized by low internal velocity dispersion, making them resistant to internal forces. A unique feature of giant ECs is that they lack interstellar gas and are primarily composed of old stars and dark matter. Data on 102 giant ECs within a specific radius showed that roughly two-thirds are oriented at an angle to the surrounding structure, while one-third are found to be aligned. Additionally, 102 giant ECs within a specific radius were used to calculate their rate of merger, based on the number that are positioned at an angle to the surrounding structure. Data also showed that objects positioned at an angle to the surrounding structure and have younger ages have smaller giant tidal features, as the fraction of light produced by these features decreases over time. The theoretical model indicates that mass objects emit two forms of bipolar outflows, which repel each other. These outflows are reflected in an ergosphere formed by the interplay of gravitation and outflow repulsion. The size of the ergosphere can be accessed, and it's noticeably smaller than that of Einstein's gravitation, using the same mass and spin parameters for a black hole like Cygnus X-1. Theoretical calculations of the accretion disks' profiles and total luminosity match the observed X-ray data from Cygnus X-1, including the observed flickering patterns and peak luminosity, without employing any empirical models or correlations. The results support the notion that azimuthally symmetric gravitational effects accurately describe the observed behavior in the binary system Cygnus X-1. The study further suggests that these gravitational phenomena could potentially be measured in highly asymmetrical gravitational systems like gamma-ray bursts or the solar system's Oort cloud. The study yields numerous testable predictions, offering an opportunity to validate the derived theory and provide new insights into fundamental cosmic processes, even if the novel gravitation effects remain unmeasurable in the given experiments. The study's findings indicate that black hole regions, from the ergosphere to the outflow zones, as well as an ergosphere characteristic of all massive accreting objects, may not be governed by Einstein's gravitation theory. We found that language models can effectively integrate visual controls as visual concepts, rather than just as text, and discovered that multiple visual controls can accumulate their effects without causing confusion. Our results also show that language models can expertly use visual controls in a manner consistent with their visual counterparts, and that the benefits of visual controls are not limited to literal interpretations. We believe that the potential for language models to utilize visual information is a critical capability, and one that should be further explored by researchers in the future. Our findings suggest that language models could potentially make use of visual aids, such as describe-the-image tasks, to tap into this capability. Ultimately, we offer recommendations for future research directions and potential applications based on the potential for language models to seamlessly combine visual and linguistic information. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a constrained, real-valued optimization problem and leverage its properties to develop AskewSGD. This method anneals the distribution parameters in a manner that ensures the quantized weights' discrete nature is preserved during the optimization process. Our algorithm's design ensures its contraction is equivalent to that of the straight-through gradient estimator, providing a guarantee for convergence. Our experiments validate AskewSGD's efficacy, showing it accelerates training, achieves lower error rates, and yields wider minimization basins compared to Straight-Through Estimation and its variants, especially on complex datasets such as CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. To grasp the intricacies of bio-inspired soft robotics, it's crucial to comprehend the fundamental characteristics of soft materials. Since these systems are often preyed upon by deformations, a prominent approach to analyzing them relies on identifying, describing, and controlling the underlying dynamics. As the field of soft robotics rapidly evolves, crucial issues related to the behavior, performance, and safety of these systems are consistently arising. For example, the spatial distribution of actuation plays a significant role in determining robot movements. Furthermore, the methodologies used to model and control these systems can either promote or hinder stability. Despite numerous recent developments, the absence of a unifying framework to address these systemic complexities has left a significant knowledge gap. To this end, the present work aims to investigate the interplay between modeling and control in soft robotics. By examining the existing literature, we have pinpointed the key features that define a model-driven control system. Subsequently, a comprehensive analysis of the state of the art and the prevalent techniques used to model and control these systems has been conducted. Through this study, the major limitations of the existing frameworks have been pinpointed, and the principal challenges facing the community have been clearly articulated. Ultimately, the insights gained from this research may lay the groundwork for the development of novel, uncharted paths to tackling the complexities of soft robotics and promoting a culture of collaboration between the various robotics subfields. Let $\mathcal O$ denote a finite, local, nondegenerate ordering on the complex vector space $\mathbb C^n$. This paper introduces the concept of "genuine symplectic group with respect to $\mathcal O$'" and "genuine Jacobi group with respect to $\mathcal O$'", forming a group homomorphism from the Minkowski Jacobi group with respect to $\mathcal O$ to the respective genuine group. Here, the Minkowski Jacobi group is defined as the group homomorphic image of the Weil-Royer group (which itself is an extension of the symplectic group over the ordered space) with the "unphysical" part of the homomorphism removed. These new groups are proven to be isomorphic to the "physical" part of the homomorphism in the case of Euclidean space for any given order, and isomorphisms from the "physical" part of the Minkowski Jacobi group to these "genuine" groups for certain orders are provided. Furthermore, the paper discusses the connection between the "genuine" and "physical" parts of the Minkowski Jacobi group in terms of "Fourier-type" modules and applies this to the specific case of Lorentz-Minkowski space where the "physical" group is well-defined. This work extends the "physical" group in the Lorentz-Minkowski case to any ordered complex space. As an application, the paper proposes methods for determining whether an $\mathcal O$-module is representable and provides representations for specific modules in the "genuine" groups of $\mathbb C^2$ and $\mathbb C^3$. These methods also yield applications to the study of "glossary of split regular local orders" and the connection between the "genuine" and "physical" groups in the "mixed" case where the "physical" group is not well-defined. Additionally, the paper proves applications to the study of "glossary of split regular local orders" and the connection between the "genuine" and "physical" groups in the "mixed" case of the Jacobi group, and generalizes a "glossary of split regular local orders" from the symplectic group to the Jacobi group. Finally, the paper applies these methods to the specific case of the Jacobi group over $\mathbb F_q$(t) for some prime t.

Most existing studies on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have focused on small-scale datasets, demonstrating impressive results in generating realistic images. However, when it comes to large-scale datasets with immense variability, GANs often struggle to produce samples mimicking real data. This difficulty is partly due to the lack of prior knowledge leveraged by these models. In our research, we hypothesize that a well-suited prior distribution can significantly be obtained from the data itself and that compact representations of hidden data patterns can greatly enhance GAN performance on large and diverse datasets. This concept is based on the idea that compact representations of hidden data patterns can provide a more accurate and holistic understanding of the variability in a dataset, and we verify this through the application of a dimensionality reduction technique. By analyzing the resulting representations, we identified three distinct characteristics that could act as a suitable prior: (1) visual aesthetics, (2) facial structure, and (3) color palette. By incorporating these findings into our GAN training pipeline, we developed a novel framework which adjusts the GAN loss function to embody the principles of these extracted patterns, thereby leading to a notable improvement in the generated images. Our approach specifically involves a novel variant of the adversarial loss, based on the distance between the generated and hidden patterns, which serves to correct the generated samples and drive them closer to the real data distribution. This effective adversarial loss, combined with the extracted prior distribution, enables our model to accurately capture the complexity and variability in a dataset. By extensively testing our method on a diverse range of datasets featuring significant variability, we observed a remarkable ability of our model to generate high-quality, photorealistic images that accurately replicated real data patterns, thereby ensuring the preservation of inherent data characteristics. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on datasets with significant variability, and the resulting generated images and code are publicly available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/amanpreet-singh/generative_adversarial_networks. We assessed the impact of our adversarial loss and hidden space conditioning on a state-of-the-art model by evaluating generated images using the Frechet inception distance, and the results show that both components played a crucial role in improving the model. The problem of fault-tolerant labeling for distance on planar graphs involves assigning integers to vertices such that the distance between two vertices' labels equals the graph's distance between them, considering edge failures. A simple general solution for any network uses $O(n \log n)$ space labels. However, Shraibman and Sudakov showed that in a grid graph, a solution requires at least \(O(n \cdot \log \log n)\) labels. Building on this, recent work by Datta recent extended this to all general planar networks with a similar label requirement. In contrast, our work presents an algorithm that provides a fault-tolerant labeling for up to half the number of vertices failing in any network with a fixed arithmetical structure, while only making a single copy of each label available. In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to both external driving forces and dissipation, using the Gaudin-zygot twin-boson model. Specifically, we calculate exact time-dependent two-particle correlation functions for simultaneously emitted and scattered photons under forced and dissipative conditions, as well as frequency-correlated two-particle amplitudes for co-emitated and annihilated photons. We investigate how these correlations change in response to the non-conserving Bose process, positive, and negative dissipation rates, and the influence of the anharmonic coupling on coherent twin-light emission. Notably, for the case of the positive dissipation rate, the real and imaginary parts of the time-dependent two-particle correlation function for simultaneously emitted photons match those of the Wigner distribution function for a single boson. Furthermore, for the case of the negative dissipation rate, the time-dependent two-particle correlation function for simultaneously emitted photons shows a rotational symmetry in the phase plane, and its real part positive and imaginary part negative, indicating an exotic non-thermal state. We also observe non-classical properties, such as an entanglement between photons, in a frequency-correlated two-particle amplitudes for co-emitated and annihilated photons, even under the influence of the anharmonic coupling. These results reveal novel quantum phenomena in a forced and dissipative Bose-Hubbard model, where two-particle correlations provide valuable insights into the quantum state of the system. Moreover, for the case of the negative dissipation rate, the two-particle correlations enable us to identify the boundary between the normal and exotic states of the dissipative Bose model as well as the critical point of the anharmonic coupling for coherent twin-light emission. Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection tasks in machine learning aim to identify results from known data distributions. Accurately determining when results come from these known distributions is essential in decision-making, but the lack of labeled OOD data limits research and practical approaches. This research addresses this issue by using the predictive uncertainty provided by Gaussian Processes (GPs) to identify OOD data. Two GP-based methods were developed to approximate GP predictive distributions with minimal requirements for labeled OOD data. Experiments on various unmodified, open-source datasets show that these approaches outperform baselines on classification and state representation tasks. Moreover, the methods demonstrated robustness to GP model inaccuracies on critical applications, such as control systems. We found that GP models can significantly impact GP predictive distributions, highlighting the need for labeled GP model data for effective OOD detection. This study's findings suggest that GPs can be used to detect OOD data and may also improve GP models by naturally incorporating OOD data detection. Ultimately, the methods presented in this research detect OOD data without the need for labeled OOD data and can be applied to improve GP models and GPs used in practical applications. 

Key contributors of this research are:
- Distributional GPs, which extend traditional GPs to incorporate multiple distributions, representing different data distributions. This allows GPs to indicate which distribution generated a given input, which is necessary for OOD detection.
- A Bayesian GP model that incorporates a prior over GP kernel parameters and utilizes a variational inference approach. This model, which utilizes a Nking-Flow variational inference structure, can approximate the GP predictive distribution and does not require an exact GP inference process.
- Another approach that utilizes a dataset priors and variational approximations to determine the GP predictive distribution. This method uses the Nking-Flow variational inference structure and relies on the assumption that results from the same distribution are clustered together in a particular stratum.
- A simple GP model that incorporates a Nking-Flow variational structure and uses an unadjusted GP posterior as a prior over the GP kernel hyperparameters. This model does not require an exact GP inference process.
- ControlGP, which is a control-specific GP model that incorporates a data prior over the GP kernel hyperparameters and predicts the GP predictive distribution.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience a form of heating. However, when the system is open, this heating can lead to more complex behavior. For example, in a two-dimensional optical lattice driven at the frequency corresponding to a specific quantum phase transition, the heating causes the formation of a localized eigenstate, similar to those seen in quantum-scarring phenomena, even when the system is open. Driving the system near this frequency causes an enhancement in the weight of this localized eigenstate in the expansion of the system's many-body states. Under continued driving, the weight of this eigenstate grows, eventually resulting in the condensation of the system's particles into it, even when the system is open. Notably, this condensation occurs even when the system is open, despite the absence of a conserved quantity protecting its formation. By parameterizing the phase of the eigenstate's wave function, the nonequilibrium dynamics of the system can be understood using a effective Hubbard model, showing that the density of its wave packet follows a nonlinear progression towards the condensation point, despite facing diffusive decay in the surrounding bath. Notably, this progression exhibits a slowdown near the condensation point, causing a form of 'intrinsic nonlinear critical slowingdown' in the absence of any symmetry-protecting principles. Overall, this research combines the concepts of Floquet heating, quantum scars, and nonequilibrium condensation to open new avenues for studying and manipulating matter under intense driving conditions. The observation of a localized eigenstate-induced nonequilibrium condensation may prove feasible using current-state-of-the-art experimental techniques. The advent of Service-based Chaining (SFC) has transformed network traffic into a predictable and scalable format. Fog nodes have further enhanced SFC performance through distributed processing. However, increased traffic in modern networks is marked by fluctuations and unpredictability, particularly in industrial settings where I/O operations are influenced by working patterns. This leads to Quality of Service (QoS) discrepancies and increased likelihood of service failures. Moreover, widespread service failures in Fog-supported SDN result in a combined fault impact exceeding individual fault levels, posing challenges for efficient fault diagnosis. Existing solutions cannot address these challenges due to rising standards of QoS and growing operator demands for fault-free service delivery. To address these issues, we present an integrated solution for Failure Restoration, Fault Prevention, and Energy-efficient Resource Management in Fog-supported SDN through distributed computing. Our approach optimizes in-service chaining quality, prevents future failures, and manages Fog and optical resources for optimal service restoration and fault prevention. We model our solution using a mixed-integer linear program and develop a algorithmic solution, evaluating its efficiency using real-world traffic data from an industrial setting. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our solution in achieving optimal results compared to baseline solutions. To further validate our approach, we simulate failure scenarios and demonstrate our solution's ability to prevent and mitigate service failures while maintaining energy efficiency. The source code for our solution is publicly available on GitHub. Using our approach, we successfully achieved a 52% reduction in Fog resource usage, 50% reduction in Optical fiber usage, and a performance gain 1.1 times that of the Google benchmark. Metric learning's pair-wise similarity learning has shown great success, and a widely used technique, the triplet loss's margin parameter, has been heavily utilized in various applications. Research has established that this triplet loss parameter controls model generalizability, but its influence is complex and affects different datasets differently. To clarify the loss function's impact, we have developed Gradient Surgery, a novel method that post-training modifies a model's gradients with a spatially adaptable margin, allowing for more precise analysis. Using Gradient Surgery, we have conducted in-depth investigations on three prominent face recognition datasets, and the results reveal intriguing insights. Specifically, we have found that a wide range of system-level factors, including data quality and distribution, significantly influence the optimal margin, rather than the specific characteristics of a dataset. Moreover, we have discovered various model-specific factors, including gradient direction and magnitude, number of hard negatives, and the impact of hard negatives, that collectively shape the optimal margin. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the necessity of thorough analytical evaluations when choosing loss functions, especially in the context of Unsupervised Learning. We hope that the Gradient Surgery technique and our study's findings will facilitate more informed decision-making in metric learning practices. We explore certain classes of quantum holographic error correction codes based on a modified version of the pyramidal code design, where the density of entanglement support connections follows specific power-law patterns in relation to the spatial distance. These code families, named hyper-invariant MERAs, exhibit exceptional tolerance to numerical simulations even at the extreme end of large system sizes, while complying with the principles of isotropic expansion. Building on the existing research into the invariant MERAs proposed by Harris and Summerfield, we significantly expand the range of accessible distances that can be handled, though we currently lack a rigorous mathematical framework to fully address this issue. Our work has implications for the creation of efficient, compact quantum computing architectures, as it enables us to approximate complex holographic error correction codes, thus facilitating the construction of quantum computing systems capable of handling arbitrary large volumes of data. Furthermore, we establish a key connection between our findings and the research of Haah's cubic code, where we quantify the relationship between the pyramidal code's error threshold and the Haah code's code rate through a parameter that represents spatial and entanglement support scaling. This interpretation also enables us to derive upper limits on the thermodynamic scaling behavior of quantum information, as captured by the quantum logarithm of the number of quantum states, where these scaling behaviors meet the requirements for the pyramidal code to function correctly, thus precluding certain types of extensive scaling. These fundamental properties govern the potential success of all quantum holographic codes. Moreover, we illustrate the critical importance of Haah code scaling behavior in determining the outcome of realistic simulated five-dimensional MERAs, where the code fails at certain distances due to thermal-like decoherence, thus underscoring its practical significance for the design of quantum holographic systems. Finally, we speculate on the potential behavior of our approximated hyper-invariant MERAs when time-evolved with a constant five-dimensional lattice model whose energy spectrum displays a power-law decay in the wavevector, where such evolution could compromise the code's exceptional tolerance, thus highlighting an intriguing connection between quantum error correction and the long-standing problem of quantum ergodicity. Our work was facilitated by the use of a unique numerical tool, named PyMera, which we developed to efficiently simulate the behavior of MERAs through the adaptation of an existing PyStochastic framework, where the main outcome of our project consists of the open-source PyMera code, thus contributing to the further advancement of quantum information and computation research. A proposed paper presents a distributed solution to the Optimal Conservation Voltage Reduction (OCVR) problem in IPS networks. The primary aim of OCVR is to enhance the network's thermal efficiency by temporarily reducing primary voltage to minimize energy consumption while maintaining reliable operation. Existing studies mainly focus on networks with only primary circuits, and those incorporating secondary circuits have relied on centralized processing due to the complexity and interconnected nature of the networks. In contrast, this paper tackles the distributed coordination of distributed generators and load response in both primary and secondary circuits through peer-to-peer messaging. By achieving seamless load transfer between circuits, the thermal efficiency is further improved. The study employs a control strategy based on distributed node-wise power flow to facilitate efficient communication and creates controllable and non-controllable groups of nodes to ensure stable operation during voltage reductions. In-line with recent standards, the distributed algorithm observes the constraints of power flow, node power balance, and Slater's condition to guarantee converged results, including locally and globally stable solutions that meet Slater's condition and the existence-uniqueness requirement. The proposed approach outperforms a centralized solution in terms of thermal efficiency by successfully decreasing the network's active power loss and improving thermal efficiency. Furthermore, the distributed algorithm allows the network's stability with reduced voltage to be assessed using the R-lines and R-nodes approach. The presented results demonstrate that the distributed algorithm can effectively reduce active power loss in the network by up to 2.8% and improve thermal efficiency by up to 1.6%. The proposed approach is validated utilizing the IEEE-123 node test network. All results are based on the original voltage as well as various degraded scenarios. We investigate online learning problems in which the decision-maker ( learner ) competes against a rival, referred to as the advisor, in a context-independent framework. The advisor's choice and the time it takes for the selection can be influenced by the chosen action. The objective is to guarantee the best possible performance relative to the advisor's performance for a given amount of plays within a fixed timeframe for any possible situation. The performance measure used here is the average rate of return, which takes into account delays, in addition to the standard outcome mean. Unlike other studies on bandits, the advisor's decision-making process is not restricted here. Assuming there is at least one action that the advisor never selects and has a finite mean reward, we prove that any approach which does not rely on prior information can achieve a performance ratio of $O(\sqrt{T \log(T)})/(\mathcal{P}^2\tau^2))$, where $\tau$ is the time it takes on average for the advisor to select an action, $T$ is the number of plays, and $\mathcal{P}$ is the advisor's reward mean. If there isn't a action that the advisor never selects, we prove that any approach which does not rely on prior information can achieve a performance ratio of $O(T^{3/4}\log(T)/\tau)$. Additionally, we prove the accuracy of the previously mentioned performance guarantees through counterexamples for both scenarios. Furthermore, we present a approach which does not rely on prior information that is adaptable to various time limitations and shows its efficiency through simulations. Finally, we prove the performance guarantees for scenarios in which the time it takes for the selection can be affected only by the chosen action. Deep into the twenty-first century, society's energy needs have resulted in significant environmental problems, primarily due to conventional fossil fuels. The 21st century has also seen a shift towards cleaner, sustainable energy sources, with the development of offshore wind energy being particularly influential. Its decarbonization benefits are multifaceted, including the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions that contribute to climate change. However, this transition relies heavily on minimizing costs, particularly the high maintenance costs of offshore turbines once they are in operation. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 functions into C code, with the capability to incorporate a proof of the translated code's accuracy by leveraging the ACL2 shallow embedding of C. The tool utilizes a breaker to analyze C code and determine if it adheres to the reasoning skills that ACL2 possesses. The tool was tested with a set of real-world ACL2 functions, achieving successful translations in the majority of cases. The tool's proofs of accuracy averaged approximately 5-6 seconds per function in ACL2, while the translation process took around 0.01-0.1 seconds for each function. The time it took to run the generated C code was directly proportional to the time it took to run the ACL2 functions, with some fluctuations. The tool was subject to a set of 304 ACL2 functions drawn from the SourceCodeMeter, with the tool accurately translating 254 of the functions without encountering any issues, while 39 functions produced incorrect C code due to execution timing discrepancies or compilation of C code. We introduce homotopy algebra as the foundation for a method that uses machines to learn topological characteristics from the phase spaces of physical systems. This phase spaces are represented by simplicial complexes, where orbits are mapped to cycles and closed curves to cycles with boundaries. The motion of the system is mapped to a continuous transformation of the phase space. To extract its topological characteristics, we apply continuous methods based on Morse theory and the cobordism theorem. These characteristics include an invariant that flows into invariants such as Betti numbers, Euler characteristics, Hausdorff dimension, isomorphism classes of homotopy groups, and the Henstock integral for cycles. In preparation for the $\psi(10.6\rm{GeV})$ factory, we've investigated the next-to-leading-order (NLO) order predictions for $J/\psi$ production within $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) via the direct process using the fixed-order technique.  We've found that the predicted NLO inaccuracies in the angular distributions are in line with the existing understanding for $B_{c}\rightarrow J/\psi X$ decays, suggesting that the NLO corrections will have a considerable impact.  Given this, fast NLO calculation methods for the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production and the associated radiative corrections are now being developed.  To this end, we've made use of the existing knowledge of $\rm{PS}^{3}$ and $\rm{PS}^{8}$ programs to devise a novel tool, $\rm{DIRHOCS}$, for determining the NLO inaccuracies in response functions in the angular distributions in $J/\psi$. We've applied the $\rm{DIRHOCS}$ tool to a number of observables that will be of interest during $\psi(10.6\rm{GeV})$ data collection, such as $|{\bf P}_{\eta_c}|$, $\cos \theta_{\eta_c}$ and $\cos \theta_{\chi_{cJ}}$.  Furthermore, nNLO corrections for $\cos \theta_{\eta_c}$ and $\cos \theta_{\chi_{cJ}}$ have been found using the threshold expansion technique.  This is the first instance where such corrections have been found, and they are found to have a significant effect on determinations of the angular distribution parameters $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$ and $A_{3}$.  As a result, these parameters have been recalculated including the NLO inaccuracies.  It is now planned to carry out an analogous study for $B_{c}\rightarrow J/\psi X$ to assess its sensitivity to the hadronization stage, and to fast NLO corrections for two-body systems.  In addition, beyond-threshold expansion techniques will be used to identify and characterise the NLO inaccuracies in response functions for three-body systems, such as $B_{c}\rightarrow J/\psi X_{3}$, with the aim of isolating the QED NLO corrections

Many users are unaware that PINs are used to prevent phishing and account takeover protection, instead believing they are essential for encrypting and verifying messages. This mismatch between users' perceptions of PINs and their actual benefits may cause users to overlook these crucial security benefits, which could ultimately put them at risk. User distinctiveness may also affect their understanding of PINs, as users who value convenience over security and are easily frustrated by requirements may view PINs as an unnecessary obstacle. Computing an integral is a fundamental task in many areas of physics that involves a straightforward algorithm. One of its applications is determining the total absorbed solar power across a device's surface, essential for simulations. The solar irradiance spectrum varies depending on location, time, and altitude, and for accurate simulations, integrating the product of a function and the solar spectrum across a given area is crucial. We present a method to apply Gaussian quadrature specifically tailored to the GEOS-5 solar spectrum, resulting in more precise predictions while maintaining efficiency. By using this method, a user can obtain the total absorbed solar power to two significant figures with minimal points, and up to six significant figures with 21 points. Furthermore, incorporating altitude into solar power calculations yields minimal gains, and therefore, for practical purposes, incorporating altitude is not recommended. This study explores how grammatical gender affects word representations within a language. We examine this question in three distinct contexts: at the general word level, the word pair level, and through Neural Network-based learning. Our investigation focuses on three languages that indicate grammatical gender: Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese. We discover that word similarities, as determined by vector cosines, are strongly influenced by gender in all the examined languages. Furthermore, using distributional semantics techniques, results show that grammatical gender significantly affects word representations, regardless of context. We observe consistent patterns of gender-related deviation in vector representations across the three languages. Our findings indicate that additional context-based statistics does not alter the substantial impact of grammatical gender on word representations. Finally, experiments with Machine Learning algorithms demonstrate improved performance when training algorithms consider word order with respect to accompanying grammatical gender cues. These results stress the significance of contextual linear combination in the fabrication of word representations. They also support the notion that accompanying grammatical gender information enhances the comprehensibility of the language. Furthermore, our investigation indicates that incorporating linear combination of context by means of Machine Learning algorithms facilitates improved word representation learning. Ultimately, these outcomes support the notion that companion grammatical gender cues play a vital role in the construction of word representations. They also suggest that training algorithms with such cues as additional performance factors is necessary. Considering the various implications at the levels of both cognitive processing and artificial intelligence building is recommended. Such implications could contribute to a more comprehensive comprehension of the mechanisms underlying natural language processing in the human brain. They could also contribute to the development of more effective and robust Machine Learning algorithms for the creation of compact language structures. Suggestions for future investigation are provided at the conclusion of the abstract. Such an investigation considers how various factors impact word representations and whether they can be trained by machines. It also allows for an in-depth analysis of how various word categories, including the grammatically defined noun categories, including both human and non-human categories, such as animate and inanimate objects, influence word representations and whether these categories are distinguishable within vector spaces. They also enable an in-depth analysis of the various factors that affect word representations and whether these factors can be trained by machines. They also enable an in-depth analysis of how various grammatical gender categories, including the masculine and feminine categories, influence word representations and whether these categories are distinguishable within vector spaces. Unlike basic object detection tasks, our objective is to accurately determine the location of objects without any explicit category labeling during training. This requires developing a training strategy that extracts pose signals from images without any pose annotations. Since annotated pose labels are often unavailable in real-world scenarios, our approach differs from standard category-level object detection methods. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel loss function using optimal pose alignment, which measures the angle between the extracted category-specific pose features and the optimized category pose vectors. This approach effectively captures category-specific pose signals without any explicit annotations. To further enhance performance, we integrate a global category pose estimator, which determines the category pose for any given image. This estimated category pose is used to optimize object position estimates through a refined loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully extracts category-specific pose signals and improves position estimation accuracy. Additionally, our approach outperforms existing position estimation techniques in various scenarios. The full details of our method, including code and pre-trained models, have been made publicly available. This code can also be employed to integrate position estimation with existing category-level object detectors. This study introduces VACA, a variational graph autoencoder designed to generate counterfactual queries and intervene in existing datasets. By assuming causal relationships in data generated by graph-structured algorithms, VACA improves upon existing models by modeling both node attributes and connections. Building upon existing variational autoencoders, VACA utilizes a single model to both encode and predict properties of hidden nodes, thereby expanding the capabilities of existing interventions. We validate VACA's effectiveness by comparing it to state-of-the-art models on both intervention and counterfactual queries for social network data, revealing significant improvements. Additionally, we employ VACA to generate answers to counterfactual questions regarding recommendations, security, and politics. We also provide arguments for the practical use of causal graph representations, highlighting VACA's advantages in terms of computational efficiency, usability, and flexibility. Finally, we address potential limitations of the model, suggesting adjustments to node generation to address issues of realistic counterfactuals. Such modifications are shown to be necessary when examining the causal representation of Twitter's influence graph, revealing, for example, that the causal supervisor avoids promoting mercy for specific Twitter users. Ultimately, the results reveal that VACA's interventions and counterfactual queries are consistent with established causal concepts, thereby expanding the capabilities of existing models. By combining the strengths of Wigner bands and quantum metamaterials, it is possible to create a wide range of quantum systems. However, to fully harness their quantum capabilities, a need arises for precise, point-by-point design, but this process is cumbersome when performed manually. Modern power grids require an advanced frequency management system that not only meets the traditional needs of traditional a.c. networks but also those of rapidly growing renewable energy sources. In this context, our research explores the potential of flying devices, such as drones, equipped with modern stabilization methods, to maintain power grid frequency within acceptable limits. These autonomous stabilization methods, known as ABMS, utilize visual feedback from the surroundings to adjust propulsion and lift to stabilize the grid frequency. To model the complex interaction between a centralized frequency signal and the dynamic response of both the traditional power grid and rapidly expanding renewable energy sources, as well as flying regulation agents, we leverage mathematical tools and derive two key equations representing the power grid and ABMS-equipped drone. Furthermore, we establish a novel criterion for maintaining grid stability through two key performance indicators, allowing us to analyze the performance of the dynamic regulation system with the aid of the Laplace transform and related complex mathematical concepts and solutions. Through a comparison of different parameter configurations, our research demonstrates that drones equipped with advanced stabilization methods can effectively maintain power grid frequency within acceptable limits, even in the presence of rapid changes, providing a promising foundation for the development of novel grid frequency control systems. These potential applications extend beyond traditional a.c. networks to include direct current and AC/DC hybrid power grid systems, offering a significant breakthrough for the stabilization of power grid frequency and potentially laying the groundwork for the widespread adoption of renewable energy sources and autonomous stabilization methods in modern power grids. To take the proposed concept to its next iteration, our team plans to demonstrate the capabilities of flying regulation agents in traditional a.c., DC, and AC/DC hybrid power grid systems, paving the way for a future experimental validation of the presented power grid frequency control model. This cutting-edge technology is set to revolutionize the field of power grid frequency control and the development of novel grid frequency control systems. Existing compression methods, based on spatial or temporal prediction using a parametric model, achieve acceptable compression performance at low computational costs but fall short in providing high visual quality when applied to practical use cases. In our study, we introduce a novel model-driven compression approach that learns the patterns of micro-aperture parallax in a plate-based light field, enabling accurate prediction of optical light field values and ultra-high compression ratios of up to 259:1 without noticeable degradation in quality. Our model utilizes a 2D plate-based tensor structure for efficient computation and can be used in real-time applications due to its low computational complexity. We validate our approach with high-quality compression results on various synthetic and real-world datasets and showcase its effectiveness in practical scenarios, such as stereoscopic and head-mounted display applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model can learn and predict patterns of micro-aperture parallax in a plate-based light field, even when the micro-apertures are randomly arranged. This graduate thesis delves into the critical topics of fairness and privacy in machine learning, with a particular focus on federated learning, which presents a compelling computational paradigm for securing data and enhancing computational efficiency by processing private datasets on edge devices. This research formalizes the concept of fairness and protects privacy in federated learning computations through distinct mathematical frameworks. Specifically, this thesis explores the implications of fairness in binary and multi-class classification tasks and safeguards privacy using differential privacy principles, demonstrating an equivalent level of utility in federated learning computations under both protection methods. Moreover, this thesis extends the application of differential privacy to federated learning computations for general multi-class classification tasks involving an ensemble of linear classifiers. Additionally, to facilitate ease of use and computational feasibility in implementing the proposed fairness and privacy mechanisms, this thesis introduces an algorithmic approach, referred to as the 'Stochastic Differential Privacy-Propportionate (SDP2) algorithm'. Experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed methods were obtained using a custom-built fuzzy label dataset and the EMNIST dataset. Finally, this thesis contributes to the existing literature on fairness and privacy in federated learning computations and outlines various avenues for further research expansion. We examine the control algorithms' performance under sparsity in reinforcement learning. This investigation yields two significant findings. Firstly, we establish the optimal policy for a control task when initial conditions are unknown. Interestingly, the results show that using known initial state dynamics in isolation has a negative impact on performance. Secondly, we clarify the conditions under which leveraging side information enhances or hinders performance. To address these challenges, we propose two adaptive algorithms. These methods adapt to missing information by incorporating a mixture model: one component accounts for known initial state dynamics, and the other is learned from available data. Notably, the performance of the control algorithms is guaranteed only when the dynamic mixture model's transition and reward estimates are trustworthy. This trustworthiness is achieved when the initial state dynamics are relatively accurate. This performance guarantee allows our methods to succeed in cases where over-reliance on side information would impede success. Moreover, under certain conditions, using side information is beneficial, even necessary for optimal performance. Numerical simulations demonstrate that relying solely on data-driven estimates can result in superior outcomes compared to utilizing inaccurate initial state dynamics. This finding is consistent with real-world observations, where human skills like walking and flying appear effortless, even though their initial conditions are difficult to replicate. To address sparsity challenges, our methods provide a theoretical foundation for controlling complex tasks like reaching, swimming, walking, and flying, and we also show that they can learn multiple skills in one attempt. Finally, the methods proposed have been successfully tested in a challenging navigation game that requires learning to move a disc towards a target in a complex environment with obstacles, and this experiment demonstrates the potential of these algorithms in the realm of partial-observing control. A Python-based implementation of these algorithms is publicly available at the repository https://github.com/samjayp/ sparse_data_driven_control. To the best of our knowledge, this repository provides the first known, public implementation of the theoretical algorithms proposed in this research, and it is compatible with the latest versions of Python 3. Nine experimental figures and three educational videos accompanying this work have been uploaded to the online repository https://samanthapundir.github.io/sparse_data_driven_control. Videos show the evolution of learning in a reaching task, and they highlight the impact of inaccurately applying initial state dynamics on performance. Moreover, they demonstrate the efficacy of the theoretical algorithms proposed in this research. A detailed online tutorial illustrating the concepts and algorithms proposed in this research is also available for the reader at the repository https://github.com/ samjayp/data

This study investigates the algebra of Toeplitz operators with complex coefficients within the framework of block Fock spaces. Block Fock space, denoted as $F^p_\mathbb{C}$ with $p>1$, can be expressed using $2n$ dimensional complex vector spaces, effectively offering additional structure to its analysis. The associated Toeplitz operator algebras are represented as degenerate Banach algebras within the conjugation of first type over $F^{p, q}_\mathbb{C}$. Additionally, when $p=2$, these operator algebras can be represented as classical Toeplitz operator algebras over the weighted Bergman space of a $2n$ dimensional complex vector, which is defined as $H^2(\mathbb{C}^2)$. As a result, when $p=2$ and $n=2$, the operator algebras can be represented as the standard Toeplitz operator algebras over the weighted Bergman space of $\mathbb{C}^4$ under the first type conjugation. The study further extends to the Hardy block Fock spaces, where it is found that Hardy block Fock spaces cannot support Toeplitz operator algebras with complex coefficients as they lack sufficient multiplication operations. Finally, an outline is provided for future research on Toeplitz operator algebras within the weighted block Fock spaces of multiple complex dimensions. The research results in this study can be verified using the methods of degenerate Banach algebra theory, which have not been employed in previous works on Toeplitz operator algebras over the block Fock spaces. The new theory offers an innovative approach to studying these algebras, where the results in this study can be seen as the first to explore the Toeplitz operator algebras over the spaces $F^{p, q}_\mathbb{C}$ with $p>1$. As a result, this research not only expands the existing theories of Toeplitz operator algebras over the block Fock spaces but also breaks new ground in the research of Toeplitz operator algebras over the weighted block Fock spaces of multiple complex dimensions. The theory of degenerate Banach algebra can be applied to continue this research, where it is outlined in the last section of the dissertation. To better understand the research, it is recommended to review the existing literature on Toeplitz operator algebras over the block Fock spaces and weighted Bergman spaces

Despite the success of static models, this study investigates the possibility of developing even more effective mortality prediction tools. We compare the performance of models with time-varying factor loadings, created using factor deep learning, to models with time-invariant factor loadings, finding that the former can provide information about past experiences and help understand the impact of recent events. A considerable amount of computational resources and environmental energy is expended on meta-learning, specifically in the context of neural architecture search (NAS). This phenomenon can be attributed to the sample inefficiency often inherent in meta-learning methods. A thorough explanation is provided for the inefficiency, and it is noted that NAS, being a real-world application, differs from pure meta-learning. Based on this insight, a straightforward and computationally efficient algorithm is developed to mitigate sample inefficiency in NAS, effectively reducing its computational and environmental costs. The algorithm demonstrates significant cost reductions of up to 96% and 76%, respectively, in experimental trials involving NAS. The potential applicability of these findings to general meta-learning methods is examined. That is, while the problem of optimizing a diverse set of parameters in general meta-learning is different from NAS, it is hypothesized that a similar approach could be used to tackle sample inefficiency in NAS without compromising its key properties. This idea is developed further into an enhanced NAS method that effectively reduces sample requirements and, consequently, computational costs. The approach demonstrates promising results in enabling the meta-learning of a diverse set of architectures with only a few trials. It is anticipated that similar methods may be able to counter sample inefficiency in general meta-learning algorithms. The enhanced NAS method also outperforms its base version in architectural innovation, and in addition to its cost benefits, it is found to surpass the base version in terms of performance as well. This is likely because the sample efficiency counter measures implemented in this algorithm ensure that the architectures it produces exhibit a more substantial level of architectural variation, and as a direct consequence, the performance difference. Similarly, the difference in performance between the base and improved NAS methods is found to be linked with the degree of architectural innovation exhibited by the latter. Importantly, the improved NAS method was found to surpass the base version in terms of performance with virtually no loss in required trials, and it is speculated that this outcome may be a direct result of the synergistic effect between addressing sample inefficiency and architectural innovation. Machine translation advancements have created a pressing need to improve the accuracy of machine translations from a reliability standpoint. To address this, a study measured the translation reliability of Google Translate by employing a novel method that examines agreement between multiple machine translations of the same text. To assess agreement, a post-hoc approach based on a reliability coefficient is applied after translating text into different language versions. This study marks the first time a reliability coefficient has been used to assess machine translations from a Bayesian perspective. To illustrate the reliability coefficient's efficacy, a practical example utilizing a dataset of translated street signs is provided. Furthermore, a study that examined translations of street signs across various languages confirmed that the reliability coefficient accurately identifies areas with the greatest discrepancies between translations. These areas are found to be those with low linguistic similarity, as evidenced by a correlation between the UCI similarity index and the reliability coefficient. To validate the reliability coefficient's practicality, a cost analysis of improving the accuracy of Google Translate was conducted. This research suggests that the reliability coefficient could serve as a performance metric for the ML models driving machine translations. To this end, a preliminary Bayesian inference is used to identify the most critical words or tokens that contribute to the greatest discrepancies between translations. This, in turn, can guide human annotators to assign uniform meanings to these tokens, thus enhancing the accuracy of machine translations. To support this, a proposal for a unified annotation platform - the Unification Platform - that allows human annotators to assign a single meaning to words with high reliability discrepancies is described. This study suggests that the UCI similarity index can serve as a useful indicator for identifying which ML models require additional data to minimize translation inaccuracies, thus improving the reliability of machine translations. To support this, a study that employed UCI is provided. To illustrate the study's results, a street sign dataset called the StreetSigns dataset is used. This dataset is chosen for its linguistic diversity, as it contains translations from 32 distinct languages. These translations are found to be highly uniform at a local level but exhibit increasing discrepancies as linguistic similarity decreases. To verify that the UCI similarity index accurately identifies languages with high reliability discrepancies, a correlation between the UCI similarity index and the reliability coefficient is established. This study also highlights several linguistic irregularities that can cause translation inaccuracies, as well as their potential solutions. To support this, a StreetSignsDataset analysis that employs the UCI similarity index is provided. To validate the practicality of the UCI similarity index, a cost analysis of improving the accuracy of Google Translate is conducted.

We investigated whether the reasons behind convolutional neural networks (CNNs) consistently outperforming traditional feed-forward neural networks (FFNNs) lie in their intrinsic ability to capture spatial patterns or if it's because CNNs' residual connections that bridge different layers in the feature space. To answer this, we trained the same architecture as a CNN and FFNN without any preconceived notions on the dataset and found that the CNN consistently performed better by a margin. Furthermore, by using the "cutout" method to force CNNs to learn to handle missing inputs, we were able to bridge the gap in performance and found that the main advantage of CNNs lies in their ability to handle missing inputs. Based on this, we deduced that the primary advantage of CNNs over FFNNs is due to their ability to handle missing inputs. We also discovered through the "lottery ticket" hypothesis that the key to CNNs' success lies in the ability to identify and prioritize the most valuable weights. Through the use of "sigmoid" and "softmax" activation functions, we were able to identify which weights were most valuable and found that the key to CNNs' success indeed lies in the ability to handle missing inputs. Our results have implications for understanding the differences in performance between CNNs and FFNNs and provide a new lens for studying the reasons behind CNNs' consistently better performance. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/sifting-out.

The expectation is that the most efficient ticket in the machine learning community will be identified through ongoing research and natural selection, ultimately yielding substantial benefits. However, contrary to initial hopes, the progression towards achieving optimal validation accuracy has been slow, with notable fluctuations along the way. By analyzing historical data from the NeurIPS 2017 Lottery Ticket Survival Challenge that involved the Search-Carve dataset, this study addresses two key questions: what percentage of ticket research and training time should be invested to yield the most benefits, and how should one approach ticket acquisition. Our research suggests that the ideal research outcome and training optimization are relatively close, around 0.2 and 0.3 respectively. In this research, a theoretical model is put forth to create a feasible quantum computer based on the concept of quantum path interference. The device would utilize two diverse types of qubits - analog qubits for representation, and digital qubits for measurement. The analog qubits convert variables into the form of plane waves, and the resulting signal is then detected by digital qubits for reading. Implementing fermionic systems and the fermionic swap gate within this hybrid computer setup has also been suggested. Additionally, a quantum emulator based on the same principles is proposed, allowing the simulation of a 6-qubit fermionic system on a small-scale digital-analog device, and gives a realistic perspective on the development of a large-scale quantum computer. The hybrid computer concept has also been put forward to create effective cluster-nuclei quantum computers. Finally, a feasibility study on the experimental creation of the hybrid computer is suggested using a pair of laser coolers and highly accurate micromanipulators. The digital-analog computer offers a promising new path in the development of quantum computing systems. The ability of the computer to efficiently process plane waves makes it suitable for a wide range of fermionic systems and potentially even cluster-nuclei systems, given the proper addition of atomic components. The research outlines a step-by-step plan for an actual device construction, utilizing the capabilities of modern laboratory equipment, and believes that such a machine could be constructed with current resources. The paper concludes with thoughts on the potential future advancements in the field of quantum computing systems. Given an abelian differential on a Veech curve, the action of its user-defined Lie algebra results in a finite number of distinct, translationally invariant cycles; the total count of these cycles embodies crucial residue information.
Research reveals that this particular moduli space features a singular locus defined by the intersection of specific divisor components; each component corresponds to a particular, already established cycle count.
The Veech curve then serves as a prototype to illustrate how a particular hyperplane liaison process influences the structure of the moduli space of abelian differentials.
Ultimately, further analysis confirms the moduli space contains an additional, dense open region, qualifying the curve as a dense, singular locus known as a Hitchin component. Moreover, the curve also exemplifies a particular class of curves, later validated as part of a broader family of curves comprising these components. The curve specifically represents a member of a new family called type $(1,1)$, characterized by curves with a first Betti number of two. The type $(1,1)$ family is seen as an expansion of the well-understood genus-two curve family; notably, type $(1,1)$ curves feature a non-hyperelliptic nature. Moreover, type $(1,1)$ curves, coupled with a particular class of curves known as Teichmuller curves, form the foundation of a new family of arithmetic curves; the intersection of these families remains an object of ongoing investigation. This study used the ALICE detector to measure a specific class of electrons within central Pb-Pb collisions. By combining results from two detectors, a clear pattern of elliptic flow of electrons resulting from charm hadron decays in the range above 3 GeV was identified, exhibiting a lower flow than electrons resulting from non-charm hadron decays. Although results showed a slight dependence on transverse momentum, they demonstrated no significant change in elliptic flow of electrons resulting from charm hadron decays as the mass of the parent charm hadron may vary. Researchers have thoroughly examined the vulnerability of machine learning models to mislead multiple samples with a single malicious example, but the quantum version of this issue remains largely unexplored. In our study, we adapted established techniques for finding universal adversarial examples in traditional ML models and successfully applied them to quantum classifier datasets. Specifically, to tackle the limitations of current quantum computing hardware, we used theoretical approaches to generate universal adversarial examples for simulated quantum development. In our simulation, we tested different scales of qubits, from 3 to 15, and found that altering a single quantum state or applying a specific perturbation to all product states could fool quantum classifiers in the majority of cases. In addition, we successfully applied existing methods for generating adversarial perturbations in traditional ML models to the quantum setting, which allowed us to determine that, on average, approximately 1% change in input states would necessitate a quantum adversary in order to mislead the classifier. Our findings reveal that quantum classifiers are just as susceptible to universal adversarial examples as their classical counterparts, which could make it challenging for these models to be deployed in safety-critical applications until this limitation is fully understood. Moreover, we provide steps for reproducing our results and suggest potential future research pathways, which are accompanied by relevant code repositories and datasets. In addition, we have extended the existing framework for evaluating adversarial examples in quantum models, which is crucial for fostering future research in this area. In particular, we have introduced a simplified variant of the adversarial risk measure, which enables the estimation of the risk associated with universal adversarial examples in quantum models. To achieve precise measurements, regulatory agencies, such as the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), enforce strict standards governing the transmitted RF power levels. These restrictions are particularly important for equipment using frequency-hopping spread spectrum, such as half-duplex Bluetooth, due to their potential for high interference levels when operating within a neighboring network. This paper documents the investigation and testing conducted to develop a novel empirical model based on deep convolutional neural networks, aimed at estimating the transmitted RF power levels emitted by Bluetooth devices. The proposed model exhibits compatibility with various channel models, simplifying the testing process, and has been demonstrated to accurately capture the energy spectrum, both in- and out-of-band, emitted by Bluetooth devices. Furthermore, the deep learning model has also successfully predicted the RF power levels within a 100 MHz bandwidth surrounding the central 2 Mbps frequency band. This achievement demonstrates a level of accuracy comparable to the established Bluetooth performance specification, with a mean squared error averaging approximately -40 to -41 dB. The success of this research not only showcases the applicability of deep learning techniques but also underscores the significance of leveraging the continuous advances in artificial intelligence to inform the evaluation and development of modern wireless systems and standards. With the ability to adapt a proprietary model to the analysis of RF signals, researchers and device manufacturers can utilize this approach to refine the evaluation of transmission standards, device certification processes, and the assessment of interference levels within cellular networks, ultimately leading to enhanced RF power level predictions. The methodology employed in this investigation may be leveraged in future research to analyze the RF characteristics of other wireless devices. The primary contributions of this research are summarized as follows. First, the study showcases a novel application of deep learning techniques to the analysis of RF signals within the context of Bluetooth devices. Second, the research introduces a testing approach that mimics real-world cellular network conditions to evaluate the performance of RF power level models. Third, the study demonstrates that the proposed model is effective across a range of channel models and remains stable despite variations in signal strength. Fourth, the study successfully estimated RF power levels within a 100 MHz bandwidth, achieving a level of accuracy comparable to the established Bluetooth performance specification. Finally, the study underscored the applicability of deep learning techniques and the significance of leveraging the advances in artificial intelligence to the analysis of RF signals and the evaluation of transmission standards, device certification processes, and the assessment of interference levels within cellular networks.
