In the transition towards decarbonization, power system models are used to evaluate various energy mix scenarios to identify the most cost-effective path to net-zero. Despite the critical role of renewable energy in power system models, they often underpredict their potential in practice. Our investigation reveals that model variables' sensitivity to changes in specific parameters is a major contributing factor to the inaccuracy of conventional power system models in predicting renewable energy integration. By introducing small, periodic adjustments into power system models, we can better understand the limits of model variables and develop more accurate indicators of grid capacity. Our research offers a framework for assessing and addressing the limitations of power system models and enhancing their predictive capabilities. Ultimately, this will enable more reliable model-based assessments of decarbonization pathways and the cost-effectiveness of renewable energy integration. Our methodology and results can be applied to a wide range of power system models, offering practical guidance for optimizing system development and minimizing costs in transitioning to a net-zero carbon economy. High levels of variable generation in power system models lead to reduced transmission and storage benefits in our analysis, which aligns with intuitive expectations. However, power system models often underestimate the potential of renewable energy integration and the benefits of variable generation. Our findings suggest that modelers can enhance their models' predictive capabilities by incorporating new variables to capture the potential of generation, storage, and grid expansion to accommodate high levels of renewable energy. Our analysis of power system models also confirms that model limitations, rather than physical constraints, generally determine the upper limits of variable generation in the system. These limitations can easily be mitigated through the inclusion of additional variables to accommodate higher variable generation. Our research further reveals that modelers can already observe these limitations in power system models through relatively small adjustments of model parameters. Our analysis of power system models and generation costs indicates that federal support for generation costs is a primary driver of model limitations, rather than geographical separation. Our research also shows that models with decentralized support, rather than top-down programs, can more effectively integrate renewable energy into the grid, particularly of the dispatchable type. Our analysis of power system models further confirms that models with decentralized support, rather of the regulated type, can already accommodate higher variable generation. Our research provides new insights and guidance for enhancing power system models to better predict renewable energy integration and its implications for decarbonization and the cost-effectiveness of generation technologies. The proof involves the application of a representation formula for the solution, leveraging properties of the Fourier transform and radial decay of the initial conditions, as well as an estimate of the solution's Grönwall-bound, which ensures sufficient decay in time for the Vlasov equation. The Poisson equation is then used to convert the system into an integral equation whose solution is shown to be well-defined globally through the application of a specific regularity theory. The major condition regarding the magnetic field can be viewed as a generalization of a recent result by Jun and Vecchi. Additionally, the presented results also imply new findings for specific systems reduced from the unbounded version of the Vlasov-Poisson-Poisson model proposed by Mel'nyuk and Pina. Specifically, the non-negative nature of the magnetic field's initial value can be relaxed to allow exponential decay bounded below by a positive number, as well as the requirement for subexponential initial velocities being sufficient instead of subexpensive velocities. Finally, the necessity of the condition regarding the magnetic field's initial values' stability is demonstrated through the construction of a specific counterexample. The constructed example involves a singularly extended solution with respect to time that shares all properties with the original solution of the problem in the class of its initial values, but the magnetic field is allowed to take any value, thus behaving arbitrarily. The counterexample's construction is based on a generalization of a result obtained by Jun and Vecchi in a recent paper, as well as an application of the requirements for the solution's regularity theory and Fourier transform's properties in the present context. The counterexample shows that the specific stability condition regarding the magnetic field's initial values' stability is required to show the global existence of the solution even when it is relaxed to the requirement of subexponential initial velocities. The Collatz Conjecture remains an unsolved problem in mathematics, which states that any positive integer sequence generated by the function f(n) will eventually reach 1. The function f(n) is defined as a sequence of operations that switch between doubling the integer n and replacing it with the half-value, alternating with the step of n + 1. The conjecture asserts that these sequences will always reach 1, but the driving question is whether these sequences are truly predictable and if it's possible to determine if a given number will reach 1. The study of these sequences includes both theoretical and computational aspects, which have led to some predictions being disputed. One prediction suggests that the numbers in a Collatz sequence bear a certain kind of inequality, while another proposes the existence of two distinct categories based on the valuing function it introduced. The current state of knowledge indicates that numbers falling into the second category always converge to those in the first, but the relationship between them remains unclear. The established predictions have yet to be proven, but they remain influential in the direction of research interests. The claims surrounding any potential solution or counterexample to the conjecture necessitate proper validation through proof or counterproof, but in the meantime they continue to drive the research and suggestibility of the problem. A crucial function in educational systems is categorizing diverse STEM documents. These documents encompass a broad range of materials including textbooks, science articles from multiple disciplines, and academic papers on specific subjects, along with instructional materials and supplementary materials like worksheets and videos. Given the widespread availability of various document types and their intricate structure, classifying them poses a significant challenge. To facilitate document categorization, additional context related to the content is required. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of enhancing document categorization in STEM by incorporating mathematical entity referencing. By specifically focusing on categorizing STEM documents into two types - 'Educational' and 'Non-Educational' - and considering the influence of contextual information, we develop a novel approach combining both token-level and segment-level categorization. To enrich the context, we build both a large-scale mathematical entity dictionary and a mathematical entity annotation system, which enables the identification of specific mathematical entities within various documents. By incorporating this contextual information, we achieve state-of-the-art results on both datasets - arXiv and Math, with the latter demonstrating superior performance due to the incorporation of the mathematical entity dictionary and the specific categorization of supplementary educational materials. To the best of our knowledge, this study marks the initial exploration of utilizing contextual information to facilitate STEM document categorization in STEM. Additionally, the proposed model is capable of not only identifying the categorization labels but also pinpointing the specific knowledge segments within these documents. As a direct result, this work offers a novel form of open-domain question answering in the realm of mathematics. To ensure the verifiable evaluation and accurate assessment of the proposed model, we create two publicly accessible annotation tools: one for annotating both the categorization and the mathematical entity, and the other for generating comprehensive answers to mathematical entity-based queries. We also make both the code and data necessary for our study accessible to the public. Ultimately, this work contributes to both the document classification and the open-domain question answering in the specific context of STEM by leveraging contextual information, while the mathematical entity-based annotation in STEM remains a topic of multilingual research requiring further exploration. The code and data can be found at https://github.com/liujch1998/MEL-EDC. To guarantee a match, researchers often create a large number of options in Stable Matching problems, which, though reasonable in theory, lead to excessive costs and the rejection of many potential matches in practical applications. This report presents an in-depth study on reducing the number of options without compromising the chance of finding a suitable match. However, decreasing the number of options at the beginning may hinder the process, so instead, we focus on making strategic choices throughout the process. Our first contribution is a simulation to determine the most effective approach for creating options over time, taking into account that some pairs are more likely to match than others. We then apply this framework to two scenarios: one where the algorithm continuously generates options based on its current matches, and another where existing matches are considered when introducing new options. Lastly, we extend our approach to use options based both on pairwise and three-way interactions. Our results show that selective matching leads to a consistent, substantial reduction in the number of options with only a minor decline in match quality. By implementing a simple time-decreasing interaction-based strategy, we can achieve nearly the same performance as generating options based on dynamic pairwise predictions while also improving stability. Finally, three-way interactions are shown to capture interactions of moderate magnitude that normal predictive models overlook, and incorporating these can sometimes increase the chances of matching even when the number of options is limited, though this primarily benefits scenarios with significant trio effects. This research is primarily grounded in empirical analysis, and we intend for its findings to serve as a foundation for the development of novel algorithms that make a conscious choice about which proposals to make. Our most successful method is now available to use under the MIT license at https://github.com/jwodzinski/strat-stable-matching. Additionally, an expanded version of this report, including additional results and code, can be found at https://www.overleaf.com/4fgcgmhfesxga. Furthermore, a companion paper titled "Interpretable Ex-Planar Networks for Stable Matching" has been published at ICML 2020 W&N, providing a more in-depth analysis. Both the code for this work and its companions are available at https://github.com-strat-stable-matching. Automatic text summarization models are typically evaluated using traditional metrics like ROUGE, which has inherent limitations in capturing semantic meaning. In response, a recently proposed framework, SummScore, has been designed to evaluate summary quality by comparing the semantic meaning of original and summarized texts utilizing pre-trained cross-encoders. The model leverages knowledge from large language models to accurately detect high-quality summaries and low-quality ones with ease, even those generated by trivial string modifications. Unlike other metrics, SummScore demonstrates improved correlation with human judgments, outperforming several existing metrics across diverse datasets in multiple evaluation settings. Furthermore, a mobile app has been developed where users can input original texts and observe the predicted summary quality scores, enabling the analysis of human preferences in relation to summary quality for training a more effective model. Ultimately, a trained SummScore model is used to fine-tune a GPT-3 language model, which then generates improved summaries with higher quality based on the mobile app's training data derived from human preferences. The corresponding code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenDongDong/SummScore. The advancement of beamformer technology has brought us closer to industry-standard self-driving cars. Yet, the self-driving community is still learning to effectively combine 2D and 3D point clouds from auto-sensing devices like LiDAR and cameras. In this research, we present a straightforward yet powerful LiDAR-camera fusion framework known as BEVFusion to tackle this issue, leveraging feature-rich 3D LiDAR beams and sharp 2D camera images. By projecting LiDAR features into camera views and vice versa, our framework easily fuses information from distinct sensory inputs from various sources, avoiding complicated coordinate transformations. Additionally, our framework uses a dynamic search range to efficiently handle dissimilar sensor distances. Despite its simplicity, our results show that the BEVFusion framework surpasses existing fusion techniques in benchmark tests, achieving top-notch results on the SemanticKITTI and LiDAR Semantic Segmentation benchmarking platforms. In 1974, Pohl and Fiorentini observed a laser-induced grating pattern in a liquid solution of rhodamine B, which was later reevaluated in 2004 by Grudinin and Peckham using a technique called holographic recording. Their research suggested that the observed interference patterns were a result of refractive index changes caused by a concentration gradient in the liquid. In this current study, the underlying laser interaction with the liquid has been thoroughly investigated. The study's key findings include a accurate numerical description of the laser-induced temperature profile, measurement of the thermal diffusivity of the liquid, analysis of the transient behavior of the temperature profile as a step-index fiber is turned on and off, and simulation of the resulting refractive index profile. These results confirm that the observed interference patterns cannot be attributed to a concentration gradient, as previously suggested. Instead, the observed laser-induced modulation of the refractive index is primarily driven by the temporal variation of the laser intensity. The experimentally measured intensity modulation and refractive index modulation exhibit a close resemblance to a sine and cosine pattern over a short distance of a few millimeters, resulting in complex higher-order diffraction patterns that have not been observed in solid materials. The predicted intensity and refractive index profiles, as well as the resulting diffraction patterns, demonstrate good agreement with the measured results, highlighting the significance of accounting for spatial and temporal intensity variations in the refractive index of liquids and their resulting diffractive effects. The study's numerical approach and the resulting predictions provide valuable insights into the behavioral and structural characteristics of laser-induced phenomena in liquids. Concluding design knowledge from user feedback is crucial in design science research.
However, manually extracting conclusions from user feedback is resource-intensive and
often impractical for large studies. This paper presents an innovative design
knowledge extraction approach, employing natural language processing and machine
learning. Analysis of 16 datasets from 7 different studies indicates that our
approach can accurately conclude design knowledge even when the initial design
decisions are changed. Despite this, our text-based model performs less optimally
when evaluating conclusion stability, likely due to limitations in our current
model. We suggest further research incorporate more advanced machine learning
techniques, such as sequential models, to analyze design knowledge sequences,
along with exploring non-text based design knowledge extraction methods for greater
accuracy. This study also outlines a framework for evaluating the stability of
concluded design knowledge and presents guidelines for improving conclusion
stability through systematic and controlled studies in the field of design science. 
This paper utilizes a structured and controlled approach to design knowledge
extraction, allowing for the integration of computational methods and human analysis.
Together, these methods demonstrate high accuracy in design knowledge
extraction, but our conclusions lack full generalizability due to our study's
controlled settings. Future studies should adapt our approach while modifying our
experiment design to fully generalize our findings. The study's source code and

This study proposes an methodology for creating complex analysis pipelines that integrate real-time and historical data from diverse, high-volume data sources. The methodology is based on the design of a stream data processing application, called H-STREAM. We examined the design of H-STREAM to better understand the challenges of developing such systems and the kind of support they require. Based on that analysis, we introduce a set of methodologies for developing these systems, focusing on the key stages of designing an application from such a design, with practical examples demonstrated through the H-STREAM implementation, built on top of Apache Flink. We evaluated H-STREAM by comparing its performance with the optimized versions of the individual components in a real-world application scenario and showed that it operates with low latency and real-time efficiency. The study further investigates how the proposed architecture accommodates diverse data types, handles exceptions, and includes a data cleaning module for managing complex analysis pipelines. We also explored the possibilities of dynamically adjusting parallelism in such systems, including an extension of the STREAM data processing model to address the underlying challenges. Finally, we validate H-STREAM against a real-world application, demonstrating that it matches the expected performance of an optimized single component even at the level of individual operators. The outcome of this study lays the groundwork for further research on optimizing system performance in accordance with the proposed design, with potential to generate valuable insights for real-time data analysis in fields like business, medicine, and science. The H-STREAM project described in this paper is now available as an open-source contribution to the Apache Flink community on GitHub (project 44200045). The project itself is the product of a large-scale data analytics application for business intelligence, with ongoing active development and maintenance. In SPARQL machine translation, translating queries from natural language into SPARQL queries is an essential task that has seen significant progress in recent years. However, conventional methods fail to fully utilize the knowledge embedded in knowledge base data, resulting in suboptimal translations. We introduce a innovative approach that incorporates knowledge base copy mechanism (KB-CM) to leverage this information, thereby enhancing SPARQL translation accuracy. The KB-CM system consists of a copy mechanism module, a replication gate to determine copy relevance, and a replication gate module to optimize utility, along with a novel ontology structure to frame the translation process. Experiments validate the efficacy of KB-CM, yielding superior results on both traditional metrics and interactive assessment, with notable improvements. Specifically, it achieves significant gains in accuracy on the BNB dataset, outperforming the top-performing model in ENAS-SPAS, with accuracy improvements of 3.0% MRR, 4.5% MDC, and 4.8% AUC. Furthermore, it achieves substantial gains in accuracy on the Geolinked dataset, outperforming the top-performing model in ENAS-SPAS, with accuracy improvements of 5.6% MRR, 6.3% MDC, and 6.5% AUC. The connection between the Askey-Wilson operators and the Chern-Simons theory, specifically regarding invariants of linked objects, reveals a hidden complexification of the Clifford algebra within a specific context. This relationship also yields a novel, direct link between the 3-manifold invariants derived from Chern-Simons theory and the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients of SU(2). Utilizing this connection, we derive a concise proof of a matrix inversion in the Askey-Wilson algebra, which had been previously described without providing a method for explicit computation. In addition, this relationship also allows us to derive a set of three matrices linked to the Askey-Wilson operators, which have specific commutative properties and are connected to a representation of the bialgebra. Notably, the 9 operators within this matrix representation include the Askey-Wilson operators, the lean Askey-Wilson operators, and an extension, which has related properties. We introduce novel deep field datasets that have proven effective in pinpointing interstellar and stellar redshifts through millimeter and submillimeter observations. Millimeter redshifts provide crucial insights into dust emission in distant galaxies and stellar redshifts enable the identification of actively forming galaxies in the early universe. To facilitate the interpretation of millimeter and submillimeter surveys, we have developed a simplified approach, dubbed "High-z Sudoku," for identifying interstellar and stellar redshifts in spectroscopic surveys. This method utilizes millimeter and submillimeter observations to create idealized spectral line profiles, simulating the emission of specific molecular lines (e.g., CO, CS, or HCN) in distant galaxies with distinct redshifts. By comparing these simulated profiles to actual spectroscopic line profiles, and assuming a perfect match in velocity and line width, our results show that this approach accurately predicts approximately 80% of all redshifts, including both interstellar and stellar redshifts, in spectroscopic surveys with high precision. Moreover, by analyzing the millimeter and submillimeter spectra in pairs, our "High-z Pairwise Comparison" method increases the prediction rate to nearly 90%. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our new diagnostic tools, we have applied them to spectroscopic line profiles in the REDCOEN dataset and the IRAM-30m List, revealing that approximately 80% of interstellar and stellar redshifts in the dataset can be accurately predicted and nearly 90% in the list. Two minimal dynamical systems, each with virtually cyclic group actions, were found with equivalent orbits for one having a fixed periodic pattern and the other not. Additionally, another example was discovered where the orbit equivalence does not apply in the same manner for free almost periodic actions by the same group. These discoveries contradict previous assumptions made about these dynamical systems. Moreover, it was established that continuous orbit equivalence for virtually cyclic group actions results in a finite index subgroup being equally equivalent, and that all such equivalences for these group actions are indeed continuous when the group actions in question possess the trait of invariance or periodicity. It was also found that when the group actions are almost periodic, the continuity of equivalences holds under a slightly less stringent condition, and more specifically, almost periodicity can be sufficient to ensure equivalence continuity when the group actions in question possess certain properties of invariance or periodicity. These findings lead to the conclusion that an uncountable set of minimal free actions by a virtually cyclic group exists such that these actions are almost periodic in nature and their orbit equivalences cannot be made continuous even if the group actions in question possess the trait of invariance or periodicity. It was also found that an uncountable set of minimal free actions by the group $\mathbb{Z}^2$ exists such that these actions are free almost periodic in nature and their orbit equivalences cannot be made continuous even if the group actions in question possess the trait of invariance or periodicity. These conclusions lead to several important and complex theorems being proven, and several of these theorems can be used to reduce several complex problems related to dynamical systems to the study of these specific group actions. Several of these theorems can be used to disprove the validity of certain assumptions made by mathematicians in the past. Finally, a list of open problems is provided at the end of the paper. Designing an observer for an unmarked epidemic process allows estimation of population states from superimposed noise. Given the inherent difficulties in observing such processes, particularly for large populations where mark generation is unlikely, there is a need for effective state estimation methods. This work establishes the fundamental principles for designing observers in marked epidemic processes, leveraging the underlying Markov processes to provide state estimation methods. To address the challenge of observing unmarked epidemic processes, an innovative approach is proposed, involving the use of an 'inverse' observer for the generation of infection marks. The combination of an observer for the population states and an 'inverse' observer for the infection marks renders the estimation problem of an unmarked epidemic process observable, enabling the derivation of optimal state estimation methods, including the Shalabi estimator. This paper showcases the application and efficiency of these methods through numerical simulations. Furthermore, the proposed methods are pivotal in the design of observers for the assessment of epidemic processes. The Shalabi estimator, in particular, demonstrates superior performance under various conditions and outperforms established estimators for marked processes, making it a highly effective tool for estimating unmarked epidemic processes. The 'inverse' observer proposed herein deviates from the conventional notion of an observer, rendering it a groundbreaking concept in the field. The proposed methods address a topic of ongoing research in epidemic modeling, providing significant contributions and insights through their application and analysis. Large graph analysis techniques, such as node representation and link prediction, have been developed using the node's local neighborhood. However, the current models are ineffective in sparse graphs due to their reliance on the complete adjacency matrix. As a result, the models fail to encircle and fill in the gaps of the incomplete graphs, resulting in poor performance on sparse graph datasets. We introduce SSNE, a node representation model tailored for sparse graph prediction tasks. SSNE efficiently uses the sampled adjacency matrix of the transposed graph, thus providing more accurate representations of nodes in sparse graphs. We transform the problem of graph sampling into a binary classification task, leveraging class weights to adjust the sampling ratio and ensuring optimal node representation learning outcomes. We implement two distinct graph sampling classes derived from binary classifiers to support SSNE and evaluate its performance across three real-world sparse graph datasets in link prediction tasks. The results demonstrate SSNE's superiority over existing models. We publicly release the code and datasets at https://github.com/duuong/SSNE. Our findings reveal that the micro-fabricated vapor cells meet 1 s pressure spikes, reaching approximately 67 Pa, in contrast to conventional cells that yield around 13 Pa. Additionally, we observe increased atom densities of up to 36% along with reduced collisional broadening of 25% for rubidium atoms emitted from the side at a frequency of 83 THz. However, the non-linear disturbance from both satellite and receiver endpoints can damage the structure of the retrieved polynomial, hindering accurate polarization state and signal intensity recovery. Therefore, an analytical expression for non-linear disturbance power is formulated for dual-polarization links, and its impact on frequency-hopping, spread-spectrum transmission is examined. Furthermore, a method for combining multiple copolar and counter-polar polarization waves is introduced to address the non-linear disturbance, and a theoretical model is developed to describe the distortion of the recovered signal intensity, alongside an assessment of the associated degradation factors in Q-factor and C-N0 for a variety of 4D formats. The research findings suggest that dual-frequency-hopping transmission can alleviate linear disturbance, while increasing transmission frequencies can reduce non-linear disturbance interference, potentially improving the performance of dual-polarization channels and leading to enhanced recovery quality of the signal's polarization state and intensity. The study also proposes an analytical method for predicting the performance of dual-polarization frequency-hopping links, serving as a basis for performance assessments and design guidelines for various formats, including dual-polarization T/π format, and D-T/π format, and others. These analysis results can be expanded to other 4D formats, offering a foundational approach for performance assessments and encouraging advancements in dual-polarization frequency-hopping links. Constructing an accurate depression detection system from social media data is a complex task, largely due to the inherent imprecision of machine learning models and the necessity of data comprising both training and testing sets that accurately reflect real-world mental health conditions. Initially, selecting relevant data can be challenging due to social media platforms' stringent privacy guidelines. Once applicable data is obtained, defining viable features that effectively encapsulate a system's training data is a further area of difficulty. Our study addresses these issues by presenting a new method for constructing a depression detection dataset and a corresponding analysis. By leveraging 14 distinct criteria based on psychological principles, we created a dataset that incorporates both contextual and behavioral information. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in detecting depression symptoms and highlight the significance of social media analysis in understanding mental health. Comparing the deposited dataset with existing datasets revealed that incorporating diverse criteria based on mental health principles yields better performance for a depression detection system. Furthermore, we observed significant improvements in detected depression levels and non-detection scenarios, leading to the conclusion that a well-constructed dataset is of considerable value in developing a depression detection system. It is anticipated that the methodology presented in this study will facilitate social media-based depression detection system development. Consequently, we are sharing our social media data set (available at https://github.com/monajamal dataset) and the detection system code (available at https://github.com/monajamal DepressionDetector), with the research community. in the insurance sector, achieving this goal typically requires an optimal reinsurance
contract.  Due to the contract's endogenous link with loss distributions and asset
levels, modeling this interaction poses an intricate challenge.  One approach to
address this complexity is to use stochastic dynamic models that capture the
interplay of pre-loss surpluses, loss distributions, and reinsurance contracts.

Recent studies have employed machine learning and reinforcement learning methods
to calculate reinsurance premiums in stochastic environments, assuming complete
state information is available.  However, real-world scenarios often involve
unobserved factors influencing both losses and asset levels, which can lead to over-
estimation of state information accuracy.  As a result, known models generally
rely on simplified assumptions regarding lacking state information.  Furthermore, even
when machine learning and reinforcement learning methods are applied, the reinsurance
premiums derived in typical stochastic dynamic models prove hard to interpret and
less reliable due to the absence of relevant state information.

In this study, a novel deep learning-based framework, referred to as Deep Bellman
Insurance, is proposed to address these challenges.  It combines the principles of
variational autoencoders and actor-critic algorithms to simultaneously learn a re-
insurance contract and a policy that maximizes profits after incorporating relevant
state information.  Our results demonstrate that learned policies exhibit higher
average returns compared to policies obtained through other methods, and that the
reinsurance premiums derived under VAE-AcC are more interpretable and reliable.  Furthermore, the analysis reveals the significance of incorporating relevant state
information in real-world applications.  Our extensive experiments also highlight
the impact of the network's architecture on performance and offer valuable advice for
practical use cases.  Finally, a practical implementation example is provided to
verify the usability of the reinsurance tool.  The code for DBI can be found at

In recommender systems, users' interactions with items are typically modeled using a collaborative-convolutional architecture, but this architecture doesn't account for a user's underlying purpose for interacting with an item in sequence. Our novel approach, Latent User Purpose Modeling (LUPM), includes an additional model layer that infers the purpose behind a user's item sequence interaction, which we found to be long-range correlated. By separating recommendation decisions into an explicit purpose modeling step, LUPM can learn more accurately represent users' reasons for interacting with items, resulting in significantly improved next-item predictions on real datasets from Amazon and Tmall. Notably, LUPM outperforms state-of-the-art models by up to 11%, and our analysis reveals that these gains come at the expense of model complexity, indicating a substantial improvement in model discriminative capacity when considering users' long-term interaction purposes, and underscoring the need for future research in modeling these purposes. LUPM is the first method to explicitly model the purposes behind a user's item sequence interactions, providing a new and novel perspective for researchers and practitioners in the field of sequence-based recommender systems. Our study not only contributes to recommender systems but also to the broader fields of natural language processing and biology through the application of our key technical method. We establish a precise minimum bound for the mean-squared error (MSE) in a low-rank matrix reconstruction and provide conditions for this bound to be tight. Furthermore, the results obtained eliminate the bias in existing estimators and are based on optimizing a generalization of the trace loss function, leading to the development of improved estimators. This study introduces a decentralized approach to designing linear multi-channel vector modulation schemes, which is essential for networked systems requiring high data transfer rates. To achieve this, we first formulate the problem of joint signal design and resource allocation in multi-channel systems with a sum power constraint and interference constraints between channels. Next, we decompose the complex optimization problem into simpler sub-problems using a novel dual approach. Each sub-issue can then be solved using the mirror-descent iterative method, which maintains the required symmetry in the dual variables. Consequently, distributed management coefficients can be generated and applied in a decentralized manner by individual nodes to tackle the optimization problem. Notably, this method does not rely on conventional channel allocation methods and allows for flexible resource allocation, while also achieving feasible and optimal solutions. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which the method converges and provide guidance on establishing the initial dual variable values. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we introduce a benchmark approach that combines standard channel allocation schemes with conventional optimization problems. Our results show that the proposed method achieves better system sum-rate values than the benchmark at various SNR levels. Moreover, the method yields feasible solutions for complex optimization problems by relaxing some of the constraints, which can then be updated at higher computational rates. This enables the method to quickly converge to a solution and prevent computational instability. Overall, the method offers the benefits of both centralized and decentralized approaches to achieving optimal solutions to complex optimization problems in multi-channel systems. Additional benefits of the method include its ability to seamlessly update its solutions without interruption and prevent stagnation in high SNR conditions. To demonstrate the practical implementation of the method, we invested significant time in numerically solving the optimization problem using a variety of approaches, which is an area of future research. Furthermore, the method could be advanced by incorporating novel optimization techniques, such as gradient-based methods, to achieve even better performance. Additionally, the method could be expanded to consider complex scenarios like node failures and malicious node attacks to make the system even more resilient. Finally, the method could be applied to a broader range of applications such as data transfer in edge networks and distributed computing, which is an area of future research. Eco-evolutionary dynamics can be observed across various timeframes, from centuries to years, and even impacting immediate ecological responses. Although existing theories and models incorporate time lags, the majority focus on single, unified timescales when in fact multiple concurrent timescales are at play. For instance, evolutionary changes that occur over long periods much slower than changes in species abundances, yet still precede ecological changes that span years to a lifetime.  These disparate timescales often interact and influence one another.  Complex feedback loops exist between them, sometimes amplifying or mitigating dynamics, or leading to instability.  We explore how differing timescales and feedback loops impact complex multi-species communities, particularly when one or more species rapidly evolves, spanning years to a lifetime.  Ecological timescales, for example population growth, predator-prey interactions, and competition, operate much quicker than evolutionary timescales, which in turn is influenced by geographical or temporal isolations that slow down or accelerate or ecological timescales, for example island biotas, different morphological or physiological attributes that affect an organism's capacity to forage, its competition with other organisms or the rate at which a predator kills an organism.  Various rate modulators, for instance river flow in an estuary, also accelerate or decelerate the ecological timescales by affecting foraging, swimming and mortality rates.  We show how converging timescales lead to amplification of eco-evolutionary dynamics, which in turn amplify or potentially reduce ecological timescales, for example population growth, which in turn accelerate or decelerate evolutionary timescales, for example rate of species replacement.  We propose a theoretical framework, for instance a tri-dimensional plot, which differentiates among time scales and their interactions, for instance deep deep history, where all time scales are distant from one another, from contemporaneous times scales, for instance long term coexistence, which may be distant from one another. Our research focuses on the performance characteristics of DEXs that utilize blockchain technology, specifically when transactions follow a decentralized, proof-of-work consensus model. Two primary factors influence a DEX's exchange rate, including the rate at which order book liquidity is restocked and the level of transaction fees, which must be balanced against the blockchain's block reward. Investigating DEXs on the Bitcoin network allows us to analyze a comprehensive range of settings, thereby distinguishing between theoretical and practical outcomes. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that there exists an optimal transaction fee level, which we term λ*, that optimizes a DEX's long-term exchange rate stability; this optimal level depends upon various parameters including the blockchain's block reward, the frequency of price changes, the speed of liquidity replenishment, and the speed at which traders execute orders. Moreover, our analysis indicates that a DEX's stability is improved when the speed of liquidity replenishment accelerates or the block interval shortens. Consequently, our study proposes a method for calculating λ* and demonstrates its applicability in real-world scenarios using actual data from a DEX operating on the Bitcoin network. Through our research, we validate our theoretical model by identifying λ* values that effectively explain the behavior of a DEX on the Bitcoin network, thereby substantiating our theoretical predictions. One key observation from our analysis is that the DEX's geometric mean exchange rate can be higher than the inflation rate, which indicates that the DEX's exchange rate stability can be enhanced by shortening the block interval. Lastly, our research outlines a series of guidelines for practitioners aiming to maximize a DEX's exchange rate stability, which primarily revolves around enhancing the speed of liquidity replenishment. This study contributes to the understanding of DEXs operations on the bitcoin network, which might inspire the development of a more efficient exchange platform based on blockchain technology using a different consensus model. For instance, consensus models such as proof-of-stake or hybrid consensus models could potentially yield the same benefits in a more energy-efficient manner. As an extension of this research, investigating the properties of DEXs that utilize consensus models with lower energy requirements could lead to a broader range of benefits. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the speed of liquidity replenishment is a critical factor for achieving optimal DEX performance, which could motivate the development of more efficient liquidity replenishment mechanisms. One such example could be implementing a fund or reserve that is quickly replenished with liquidity to enable swifter order execution. Additionally, our analysis could inspire future research on optimizing DEX operations by identifying λ*

Determining the influence of uncollected data in observational studies is a critical research issue. We developed a novel Bayesian approach to quantify the weight of uncollected survey data, utilized missing data prediction models in Bayesian analysis, and established a measure of uncertainty impact resulting from uncollected data, referred to as E-m, based on the proportion of uncertainty attributed to the missing covariance matrix. An analysis of data from the National Health Interview Survey measured the impact of uncollected data on prevalence estimates of major chronic diseases in the US. We compared four Bayesian regression models, including stepwise regression and regression integration, to address missing data. E-m assessments indicated that uncollected data from high-prevalence diseases influenced analysis results for other diseases, with larger E-m values associated with regression integration and lower levels of missing data. This study introduces a Laument extension of quantum surfaces based on the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra. We categorize its key elements: quantum analogs of elliptic curves, rational functions with poles, and two distinct differential-difference operators which we prove are interrelated via Drinfeld's twist. We also demonstrate that the operator corresponding to a rational function's Laument extension depends solely on its poles and residues. Notably, we identify a subset of non-singular elliptic curves that maintain $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ symmetry; this set includes certain well-known integrable systems such as the Toda molecule and the Rabi model. Moreover, we illustrate that Drinfeld's twist can be utilized to induce $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ symmetry from a known $U_q(\mathfrak{sp}_4)$ symmetry of the Toda molecule. Our findings significantly expand the scope of known $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-integrable models. Moreover, we propose two new model types that likely possess $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)\otimes U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ symmetry, namely the two-mode quantum Calogero model and the two-dimensional Lipkin model. Interestingly, all known $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetric elliptic curves feature two distinct non-trivial cycles; this characteristic distinguishes them from Drinfeld's twisted curves, which possess a single cycle. Lastly, we show that the Laument extension of rational functions, unlike those obtained via the quantum harmonic analysis method, do not preserve the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra action. NuSPAN consists of two key components: a sparse convolutional network that extracts features from raw data with a sparse pattern and a proximal average network that learns and replicates sparse patterns from limited observations, ultimately producing high-quality inverted results. To validate its effectiveness, we applied NuSPAN to a seismic inversion problem and compared its performance with leading sparse optimization techniques, finding that the method not only acknowledges the actual sparsity pattern but also achieves superior data fitting and parameter recovery outcomes. Our experimental results demonstrate the potential of NuSPAN to be a user-friendly, assumption-free approach for tackling various inverse problems. What's more, the method is capable of not only improving data fitting and recovered parameters but also understanding the underlying sparse pattern. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between sea surface temperature, wave height and pressure is examined, linking them to the spatial extremes of the 1990-2009 average. A model of this type identifies the dependence structure of extreme events, with the wave height pressure having the greatest dependence on extremes (around 0.7) and sea surface temperature having the least (around 0.3). This pattern holds across various locations in the North Atlantic. When analyzing the Bay of Fundy, a region known for its intense waves, a significant increase in the extreme sea surface temperature, by as much as 2.5 standard deviations, was found to be associated with extreme wave heights, resulting in a 35% increase, while sea surface temperature and wave height also showed a 37% and 23% increase respectively, when compared to typical conditions. Similar analyses were conducted for other locations in the North Atlantic. Furthermore, using historical data from the 19th century, the study shows that a decline in sea surface temperature, by as much as 2.5 standard deviations, was associated with extreme wave heights, resulting in a 18.5% decrease, along with a 13% decrease in sea surface temperature and a 23% decrease in wave height. Results from the analysis of the North East Atlantic, covering the period of 1979-2019, show consistency with historical data from the 19th century, in addition to significant changes in the relationship between sea surface temperature, wave height and pressure in the Bay of Fundy. The pressure at Barbados, a island located in the South Atlantic, was found to be less sensitive to extreme wave heights, by around 30% compared to typical conditions, while a decline in sea surface temperature, by as much as 2.5 standard deviations, was associated with a 15% decrease in wave height. The study highlights the need for spatial modeling in the analysis of marine extreme events. Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, the absence of guidance hampers its potential for task-specific adaptation, and including extensive manual labelling of data attributes becomes necessary. To address this limitation, our VT-CLIP approach introduces an additional step of joint learning, where visual cues are guided by corresponding text attributes. This is accomplished by contrasting the visual and text attributes separately before uniting the two for joint learning. Experiments on multiple semantic segmentation and visual question answering datasets demonstrate VT-CLIP's effectiveness in leveraging visual cues from attribute-based guidance without requiring substantial fine-tuning adjustments. Furthermore, our results highlight VT-CLIP's adaptability on a range of tasks, and our code is made publicly available for reproduction. Our findings suggest that incorporating guidance from pre-defined attribute texts can effectively reduce the requirement for manual data labelling in CLIP-based models, thereby facilitating the development of more scalable models for precision tasks. At the same time, our results show that eliminating the guidance step can still yield comparable or in some cases improved performance on CLIP models, such as CLIP:ViT-32. Its relatively weak control over visual representations from raw data suggests considerable room for further research in refining these representations through attribute-guided control in the Visual-Language space. To this end, our study presents different training and evaluation protocols for attribute-guided CLIP models and provides a systematic assessment of their performance. Ultimately, our VT-CLIP approach offers an essential step towards developing models for Explainable AI, where visual representations can be generated with precise control from multi-modal inputs. By expanding the capabilities of CLIP models, our technique facilitates the construction of models with similar attributes to generate coherent and relevant visual representations, even in the absence of direct supervision. Such attribute-directed control in the Visual-Language space presents an exciting area of research for the development of more interpretable and robust models for computer vision at large. This paper showcases an unsupervised method that applies self-supervised learning to train deep neural networks on an entire DNA dataset without any labeling, achieving this through the implementation of a new autoencoder on entire sequences. Our experiments conducted on diverse DNA datasets confirm our initial hypothesis that unlabelled data can effectively capture universal characteristics present across various classification tasks. Additionally, our study highlights several crucial factors that influence the performance of unsupervised methods on distinct datasets. These results indicate that deep neural networks can automatically extract general and useful characteristics from unlabelled data, facilitating their successful transfer to various tasks and datasets. These methods can therefore alleviate one of the major limitations of supervised learning by eliminating the need for extensive and expensive data labeling. Our work also demonstrates that successful unsupervised methods can be extended for feature enhancement across a range of tasks and datasets by adjusting a key hyperparameter in our proposed method. In the current COVID-19 pandemic's context, accurately diagnosing patients and rapidly isolating infected individuals are critical aspects. Radiological findings from CT scan analyses play a pivotal role in diagnosing COVID-19, highlighting the need for rapid detection through CT scans. However, conventional capsule networks exhibit spatio-temporal and rotational invariant properties, which can sometimes impede fine-grained local representation learning, a crucial capability for diagnosing COVID-19 from CT scans. Moreover, standard capsule networks treat individual capsules as separate entities, which increases training complexity. To address these limitations, a new method called TLDCN is proposed. It leverages an orthogonal projection mechanism to preserve capsule relationships, thereby enhancing local representation quality. Additionally, a new time-distributed capsule network model is designed with two stages, using spatial and temporal capsules in tandem to capture precise diagnoses. Our TLDCN model, implemented using a 128-layer CNN architecture, successfully achieved an accuracy of 98.33% on an interinstitutional dataset, demonstrating its efficacy in diagnosing COVID-19 from CT scans. Furthermore, experiments conducted with datasets collected from multiple institutions revealed the model's interinstitutional generalizability, demonstrating its potential for widespread application in real-world diagnosis settings. Based on these results, it is envisioned that our TLDCN model will be extensively utilized in various applications, such as AI-assisted diagnostic systems. The source code for this research has been made publicly available. With further advancements, this model may be adapted for use in other medical imaging domains, such as detecting lung tumors or cardiac disease from 3D CT scans, representing a highly promising area of investigation. A future research direction could involve developing this model using multi-modal data, such as combining CT scan data with positive/negative labels and CRAG scores to improve detection accuracy. A novel approach has been introduced to compute the Sinkhorn iterate in O(n) time complexity by leveraging the properties of triangular matrices. Additionally, a more precise method for computing the kernel function has been proposed, accurate to a specified level of rounding. By combining these improvements, new algorithms named Fast Sinkhorn II have been designed, comprising two versions that utilize Newton iteration to obtain a more precise solution in O(n) time: a direct algorithm and an iterative one. These Fast Sinkhorn II algorithms have been proven to exceed the performance of conventional Sinkhorn algorithms in all aspects, achieving up to a 10 times speed increase while producing a solution with a solution gap of at most 1.5 times the optimal value. Moreover, the algorithms were found to be scalable in practice, with running times, in some cases, taking only as little as two microseconds to execute. To validate the algorithms' performance, comprehensive numerical experiments were conducted to demonstrate their efficiency and solution quality. Importantly, the algorithms preserve the first-order optimality conditions of the optimal transport problem in full precision, as demonstrated by the fact that the gradient of the composite kernel function is computed with a level of rounding specified by the user. To facilitate the implementation of these algorithms, which have been designed using a row-oriented approach, detailed code based on C and MATLAB has been provided, including advice on handling edge cases and specifying the level of rounding for the user. Finally, the algorithms' performance and solution quality have been found to be robust in practice, with the results of numerical experiments conducted using 12 diverse datasets, revealing very small gaps between the solution value and the actual optimal solution in all cases. To counter this issue, we suggest a modification to the standard nearest neighbor classification method. By training a conditional diffusion model with motion data label information, we develop a technique that generates realistic and high-quality moving images. Unlike traditional models, which typically fail due to sensitivity to hyperparameters and low sample data, our approach successfully achieves high-quality results using only approximately hundred motion-annotated sample data. By accurately replicating the static-to-moving transformation in the latent space, we demonstrate strong image reconstruction results from both canonical position and during motion. Furthermore, our method excels in the creation of artificially extended moving sequences with just a few reference frames. We conduct rigorous evaluations on diverse datasets to guarantee generalizability, showcasing its potential in the creation of both training datasets for computer vision and reference material for human observation. The effects of this generated content are demonstrated in depth-flow maps, which reveal new information about the movement of the subject. However, current model-based methods rely heavily on system equations and initial values, which can be time-consuming to obtain and may not always be available. To address this limitation, data-driven approaches have been developed to predict, optimize, and control complex systems using historical data alone. Despite their potential, current data-driven methods are often only applicable to specific problems and cannot be used for control decisions. To resolve this issue, we propose a new data-driven framework that can be used for prediction, optimization, and control of complex systems. Our framework consists of three main steps: first, we generate data sequences using the historical data; second, we apply a sequence of neural networks to calculate the optimal control input for a given state input; third, we use the optimal control input to evolve the system. Our framework was successfully applied to the networked SIS epidemic model. To test its validity, we used actual city data to predict, optimize, and control real-world epidemic models. The results show that our framework produces effective and logical control strategies that can be used for prediction, optimization, and control of complex systems. Additionally, our framework can be extended to address more complex issues. Specifically, we applied our framework to three real-city cases, demonstrating its potential in tackling complex system control problems. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architecture, comprised of separate encoders and decoders, has recently been of great interest due to its capacity to improve model robustness. However, current implementations of MIMO often adopt identical or nearly identical encoders and decoders, which hampers its ability to harness diverse representations. Inspired by the success of communicating gradients in multi-agent co-training, we suggest an innovative symmetric model sharing approach for MIMO, where shared encoder and decoder use opposite gradient communication: the encoder shares its weights via reverse gradient optimization, whereas the decoder shares its weights via regular gradient optimization. This method is experimentally validated across multiple scenarios and datasets, revealing substantial boosts in robustness and adversarial resistance for MIMO architecture. The method's benefits are also mathematically substantiated. Experimental results further indicate that our proposal outperforms conventional models under multiple conditions and demonstrates greater generalizability. The code for this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ongoingic/symshare. Our study and findings suggest that adopting distinct encoders and decoders is suboptimal, and symmetric model sharing provides a versatile and effective framework for improving MIMO architecture robustness and resilience. This interaction is typically modeled using density functional theory, with practical implementations using two main approaches: the decoupling scheme and the interface method. The decoupling scheme, incorporating the modified Stokes-Einstein equation, is widely employed due to its straightforward implementation and moderate computational overhead. Although the interface method, using general coupling equations, yields more accurate results but with increased computational complexity. This work presents a novel, high-accuracy integration scheme, the Multi-Center Integration Scheme, to be used with the interface method. By improving the integration technique, the interface method can now rival the decoupling scheme's efficiency while providing more accurate results. Numerical experiments demonstrate the M CIS's ability to maintain stability and convergence in diverse scenarios, where M CIS's accuracy was proven in comparisons with the multi-scale lattice-Boltzmann method in a specific case study. Moreover, M CIS's results were verified for consistency with physical principles in a study of gas flow around a moving disk using the Navier-Stokes equations for comparison. Finally, the M CIS's performance is evaluated in a comparative study of gas flow within a cylindrical shell, where it shows more internal consistency than traditional methods, leading to more reliable outcomes. These studies together show that M CIS's innovative physics model can yield accurate and reliable results in a wide range of gas-flow simulations. This M CIS approach not only enhances computational efficiency but also provides a more accurate understanding of the underlying physical process, thereby facilitating a more reliable modeling capability. This study suggests that M CIS's integration technique has the potential for broad applications in physics and engineering fields where reliable gas-flow simulations are critical to theoretical and experimental efforts. Moreover, the development of M CIS indicates that increasing computational complexity can be effectively used to improve accuracy in simulations, as shown here with the improvement of M CIS-based interface method simulations relative to the decoupling scheme. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, pandemic severity, and news audience. Using 395 stations spanning 100 markets covering 78% of the U.S. population, researchers found that local news mentioned COVID more frequently in the final pandemic stages. Market-level COVID cases and deaths were associated with increased COVID coverage. Interestingly, when COVID was covered more extensively, local news also devoted more time to other social issues, suggesting intercorrelations among a news station's topics of interest. Moreover, COVID coverage was linked to a diminished local news audience, both in terms of actual viewers and perceived news trust. These results imply that COVID coverage by local news is in sync with pandemic severity but negatively affects its own audience, potentially harming the news station's reputation and visibility. Ultimately, this study underscores the significance of local news in addressing public health issues. It also emphasizes that local news stations need to strike a balance between highlighting critical national and global issues, like the pandemic, while maintaining a strong connection with their local audience. At the $Q^2$ value of 0.1 GeV$^2$, the polarization transfer from a initially polarized proton to the final proton is found to be $8.39 \% \pm 0.23 \% \pm 0.31 \%$, with the first error stemming from statistics and the second from the overall $A$ and $D$ errors. These errors also include the impact from the uncertainties in the proton's elastic form factors. The results are in line with the longitudinal-electric or longitudinal-longitudinal magnetic photon proton interaction cross-sections. They are also compared to the results from the CLAS, CENPA, Jefferson Lab measurements and the theoretical predictions from the charge-conjugation invariance theory and the generalized parton distribution functions. Teaching machines how to solve complex problems by using other experts as guides has proven successful in the past, for example, showing a patient the correct way to do an exercise. However, this approach can be time-consuming and inefficient if the machines need to spend time in the early stages learning the basics. Typically, machines are trained using large datasets of problems, often obtained randomly, to accelerate the learning process, by teaching them the fundamental principles first. Distinguishing between genuine data and artificially created data that has been generated by machines is, however, a difficult task. Our proposal involves generating additional data, referred to as pseudo-data, to aid in the learning process, by tweaking the outputs from expert advisors while keeping their solutions applicable in real-life situations, thus improving learning efficiency. We implemented two methods to achieve this: adjusting policy outputs to fill gaps in the solutions and manipulating the solutions directly to improve learning performance. Our test using reinforcement learning as an example revealed that utilizing pseudo-data resulted in significant improvements in the machines' ability to solve challenging problems efficiently. Our research found that these generated datasets, which are classified as synthetic, can be combined with authentic datasets to boost the efficacy of machine learning. Additionally, our methods allow the incorporation of domain-specific knowledge to guide the generation of pseudo-data, even when this information is limited. Our proposed techniques can thus accelerate the learning process and improve performance by tailoring the machines' initial learning experience to specific requirements. Finally, our research reveals that synthetic datasets hold promise as a valuable tool in customizing machine learning. Our paper presents a comprehensive overview of the challenges associated with the initial stages of machine learning, proposes the utilization of pseudo-data, and provides guidelines on how to generate this data. Our research further examines the advantages and limitations of synthetic datasets, as well as the challenges associated with their creation and incorporation into authentic datasets, and discusses their future potential in customizing machine learning. being restricted by a fixed set of classes. The anomaly detection track focused on
the ability to identify samples that differ from everything else. In total, over 70
participants and 165 team members submitted entries to two tracks of the challenge
(Out-of-Distribution and Anomaly Detection), submitting more than 300 team members.
The challenge introduced two novel innovations: introducing transfer learning as an
essential factor in OOD challenge evaluation and providing access to private datasets
for practical training. The outcome of the challenge revealed the limitations of
current representation learning methods, likely due to the tension between
generalization and bias. The issue is complex and requires the integration of
expertise from bias and out-of-distribution detection, along with an enhanced
understanding of the nature of learning itself. The result of the challenge
highlights the importance of leveraging transfer learning effectively. The issue
will be further investigated, and the solution may involve pre-training strategies
that create versatile representations, complemented by local inference methods that
account for local conditions, potentially addressing the gap between the two. 

The issue is particularly prominent in the context of out-of-distribution and
anomaly detection, given the inherent bias and rigidity of in-distribution
learning objectives. The challenge may be overcome through the integration of
additional loss functions, more diverse data mixing, and improved attribution
methods that reveal the decision-making processes of the model. The outcome of the
challenge may serve as a starting point for the next steps in the development of
effective out-of-distribution and anomaly detection solutions. The issue and its
solutions and implications will be further explored, and the discussion and next
steps will be shared at ICML 2023.

This research investigates whether shortest paths exist between two random points on the manifold formed by a Gaussian random field, and under what conditions these paths are uniquely defined. It is demonstrated that the existence of these paths is largely determined by the negative minimum eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, and that the presence of at least one positive eigenvalue is not a necessary criterion for their existence. To find the shortest paths, a stochastic differential equation is employed to derive a Kolmogorov equation, which is then approximated using Monte Carlo simulations. These simulations reveal that the geodesic method is accurate in most cases, but subject to some limitations, due to the potential for multiple geodesic paths and path regularization. Nevertheless, the method is found to be a valuable computational tool for approximating the shortest paths, and that their existence is, in some cases, guaranteed. Furthermore, it is proposed that the geodesic method can be used to determine conditions under which these paths are guaranteed to exist. Exactly what conditions the covariance matrix must satisfy in order to ensure their existence is explored, as well as how the nature of the field itself impacts its existence. To this end, it is discovered that fields featuring at least one positive and one negative eigenvalue of the covariance matrix are those for which these paths are guaranteed to exist. Finally, the research concludes by highlighting geodesic paths' relevance to various applications, including optimal transportation, computer vision, biology, physics, engineering, economics, and social sciences, and proposes that their existence is, in part, a measure of the field's structural informativeness. As such, it is suggested that the existence of these paths represent a structural criterion for assessing Gaussian random field informativeness. The research then concludes by framing the problem of detecting a field's structural informativeness and identifying the most structurally significant features as an open and unsolved problem. The problem is proposed as an addition to future research, and the researchers aim to pursue its solution in their next work. Our research focuses on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on urban dynamics by analyzing how people's daily routines changed in response to economic conditions, finding varying levels of activity in different income groups. To make this analysis possible, we created a data-driven platform to estimate everyday encounters in urban environments based on individuals' movement patterns. According to our findings, lower-income individuals generally maintained more consistent activity patterns throughout the pandemic, whereas higher-income individuals exhibited greater changes in their daily routines. Consequently, our simulation indicates that the diversity of encounters in urban centers experienced a significant decline, particularly affecting lower-income groups who saw a reduced variety of people they encountered. Conversely, higher-income individuals reported a slightly increased diversity of encounters. To further explore these outcomes, we conducted a case study in Madrid, comparing the diversity of encounters in different neighborhoods, which showed that low-income areas experienced a more pronounced decrease in diversity during the pandemic. Our results suggest that urban centers with greater income inequality tend to be more resilient to external disruptions, whereas urban areas with more uniform socioeconomic conditions are more susceptible to changes in urban dynamics, ultimately requiring careful urban planning to maintain healthy and diverse urban ecosystems. As robots increasingly co-work with humans in the same physical space, the need to follow established social norms to promote safe and efficient collaboration grows.  A key robotic "etiquette" rule suggests that to maintain a safe distance from others, robots should keep a distance of at least one and a half to two body lengths away, much like how people typically aim to maintain a 1.5 to two meter distance from one another. This work introduces a novel variational framework for simultaneously image reconstruction, sensor noise alleviation, and material analysis in CT scans, where different x-ray sensors with varying energies and detectors record different signal patterns. By formulating the task-adaptive CT reconstruction as an energy minimization problem that incorporates prior knowledge, we can tackle such tasks as identifying bound metal screws, detecting stainless steel screws, or distinguishing between PEEK and carbon fiber materials. To achieve these goals, we adopt a dual formulation of the constrained least squares problem, leverage existing solver developed for image reconstruction, and further regularize with data-driven priors to obtain enhanced results. To evaluate the performance of our approach, we created a test bench with synthetic and real-world data featuring screw threads, carbon fiber materials, and industrial objects such as aircraft parts. We compared our results with the state-of-the-art task-adaptive CT (TACT) method and found that the proposed variational framework achieves superior outcomes, accurately reconstructs polyenergetic CT signals, effectively removes sensor noise, and provides accurate material information. We investigate how different quasiparticle theories, including RPA and TDA, predict behavior in the limit where the gap between two metallic regions becomes very small. Our analysis indicates that when the gap is negligible, an RPA description yields plasmon dispersion that deviates from both TDA and the true QEDC perturbation series. Specifically, the low-frequency mode in the coupled system undergoes quadratic rather than plasmonic-like dispersion. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions from Magnetic Resonance images is essential for disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and assessment. Recent studies indicate a discrepancy in segmentation performance between hospitals due to varying data quality and scanning protocols. In this paper, we investigate two approaches to tackle this issue: training models from scratch using annotated datasets from the same distribution, and maintaining a reference model through continuous learning across similar distributions. Our study involves four hospitals, providing a robust benchmark for MS lesion segmentation that reflects real-world data diversity. It also includes a simulation to mimic a scenario where reference models are unavailable. These simulations show that using a reference model yields a 2.14 m^2 improvement in Dice score compared to training models without it. Moreover, our results indicate that learning continuously from scratch achieves comparable results to utilizing a reference model, while also outperforming training models without any adaptation on MS lesion segmentation. To the best knowledge of our knowledge, this study is the first to compare these approaches extensively. Our findings also highlight that training models without a reference is challenging, even with large datasets, given the simulation's results. These datasets' diversity allows the models to learn from datasets with distinct characteristics, mimicking real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our study's results can contribute to improving the MS lesion segmentation process, ultimately benefiting patients' clinical assessment and treatment. As an example of potential applications, using these models on T1+GAD scans from the NEUROBANK dataset reveals that NEUROBANK's lesions match two hospitals' lesion distributions closely, paving the way for data collaboration between institutions. Research on contrast in visual media is generally associated with the extreme case where objects of interest differ from their surrounding environment in terms of brightness, as is typical for objects against a background. This study explores the uninvestigated midpoint of the contrast continuum, where objects of interest exhibit intermediate brightness levels relative to their surroundings. Our objective is to understand the perceptual impact of this "bipolar contrast" by providing the first systematic characterization of images featuring objects of variable brightness and assessing human viewers' responses in categorization tasks. Our findings indicate distinct visual processing patterns for high-visibility contrasts (distinguishing objects from their backgrounds) and low-visibility contrasts (distinguishing objects of one another), where information from each is incorporated to differing degrees. Additionally, our experiments have identified methods for quantifying bipolar contrast effects and have revealed that human brain activity, as measured through EEG, correlates with these effects. Our proposed model is designed to account for observed human responses and suggests that bipolar contrast applications can be optimized based on both human cognition and neural function. Our research demonstrates that bipolar contrast is a crucial factor not only for enhancing human performance but also for reducing fatigue and electrophysiological exhaustion. A software implementation that enables the creation of bipolar contrast effects in images and videos is publicly available at https://github.com/bipolar-contrast. High-dimensional dynamic time-series data can be efficiently analyzed using cross-sectional econometrics, but the field remains largely non-theoretical and unreliable due to the numerous possible model specifications. By focusing on a subset of these models, including vector autoregressions, this paper provides an in-depth examination of the methodology and offers suggestions for future research directions. Notably, the literature often neglects key assumptions of linear or exponential error terms, and this oversight impedes the application of asymptotic theory in high-dimensional settings. Nonetheless, the paper makes a case for a theoretical framework based on standard statistical principles and, given the numerous applications of dynamic modeling, aspires to establish a reliable foundation for high-dimensional time-series analysis. Key areas for further research include the development of theoretical connections between dynamic modeling and principal component analysis, the exploration of the causal implications of model specifications, and the potential extensions to non-stochastic scenarios. Additionally, the paper touches on the intersections between high-dimensional dynamics and machine learning, as well as the need for more experimentation in simulated data environments. Ultimately, the paper aims to establish a unified theoretical framework for high-dimensional dynamic cross-sectional time-series analysis and serves as an entry point for scholars new to the field, while identifying essential avenues for further research in the discipline's development.
