Developing gyrokinetic quasilinear theory enables the reduction of a multi-dimensional plasma state to a lower dimensional form, ignoring non-resonant waves. This simplified model, known as the turbulent diffusion equation, effectively predicts plasma saturation levels and mixing rates. Our work develops a novel numerical tool based on the finite element method to solve the quasilinear diffusion equation. By constructing specific discrete spaces and assembling the corresponding matrix, our method conserves key properties of the original equation such as positivity, energy, and the magnetic invariants. Moreover, our approach ensures the accurate solution of the linear problem in the discrete world, including the correct prediction of maximal and minimal values. To validate our method, we perform thorough numerical tests to assess its reliability and accuracy in modeling realistic solar coronal turbulence. These experiments examine (i) the characteristics of the discrete solution in a variety of finite element meshes and (ii) the quasilinear diffusion equation's behavior under realistic solar conditions, assuming a constant index of refraction. Our results compare well with existing literature and provide valuable insights into the quasilinear process. We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions to the Lyapunov equation in a Banach space. Specifically, we show that for weakly sectorial generators A, a bounded and continuous Lyapunov function ϕ that characterizes the resolvent R(λA, I) will, when certain conditions are met, lead to an explicit bound on the norm of the semigroup T(t) and prove exponential stability of T for any α with |Re(λ)| < α. This result generalizes previous work in Krein and applies to positive operators as well as generators of cosine functions, offering a straightforward approach to proving stability in Banach spaces. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of this method by demonstrating its application to stability analysis of abstract reaction-diffusion systems in the MHD example. To show the relevance of the Lyapunov function to the system, we use the Birkhoff-Kelvin theorem to establish its bounded and continuous nature. Additionally, we discuss the role of the Lyapunov function's imaginary part in the context of the Birkhoff-Kelvin theorem and present an example of a function that, while bounded and continuous, falls short of the requirements of our theorem. We also demonstrate that generating a C0-semigroup by compact perturbation is insufficient to test the conditions of our main theorem. Lastly, through the system of ordinary differential equations, we demonstrate that increasing the dimensionality of a system can compensate for the shortcomings of a Lyapunov function, allowing the application of our theorem even in one-dimensional cases. Our work ultimately contributes to the understanding of the interplay between the characteristics of a space, a semigroup, and a Lyapunov function in the context of the given problem. Despite the presented generalization, we recognize that the specific conditions of our theorem remain the object of further research in the realm of stability analysis in Banach spaces. The presented findings, therefore, provide a starting point and a goal for future investigation. MuMuPy employs Geant4-based physics lists to simulate dimuonium formation, as well as particle tracking within simulated substance environments. MuMuPy is planned for use in further investigations of dimuonium interactions, including experiments at RHIC and future muon colliders. Upcoming enhancements will incorporate a code refactoring for improved modularity, the addition of user-friendly graphical visualization capabilities, and an investigation of code integration for use in the SHiP experiment. Evaluation of MuMuPy's performance reveals non-uniform reconstruction efficiency across transverse and longitudinal dimuonium detection areas, potentially resulting from differences in geometric reconstruction and acceptance. By simulating dimuonium production within stationary targets using the PHENIX geometric analysis, the program has identified a dimuonium reconstruction efficiency ranging from 50 to 70% along the transverse direction and 10-40% along the longitudinal direction for a specific target material. Furthermore, the program has found that the PHENIX geometric analysis yields a 10-20% longitudinal efficiency at the minimum, although it offers 50-100% transverse efficiency. To achieve the desired detection goal of 90% dimuonium reconstruction efficiency, additional muons in the simulated solution would require the use of a muon filter to select muons originating from dimuonium, resulting in a 90% overall efficiency. A central challenge facing researchers and practitioners is finding and engaging data workers who possess the qualifications necessary for precise and cost-effective data collection.
We investigated this issue by recruiting worker recruits, each of whom was hired for $5 to compile English language usage guidelines.
Our primary objective was to evaluate the cost and quality of data collected from established MTurk crowdsourcing platforms as compared to alternative recruitment methods.
The results showed that MTurk workers produced significantly better guidelines at a lower cost when recruited through established processes that utilize qualification systems and work feedback.
As a novel approach to identifying skilled data workers, we also assessed the ability of machine learning models to predict worker performance based on text characteristics and recruitment criteria.
The results indicate that, while these models can provide some insights, they are not yet reliable enough to replace established recruitment methods.
Ultimately, our study highlights the complexities involved in data collection and recruitment, and we propose that further studies from both academic and industrial perspectives are necessary to address these challenges.

Text clip retrieval, which emerged as an alternative to text encoder similarity, offers efficient and real-time video question answering capabilities by only extracting and processing key frames. However, existing text clip retrieval approaches are hindered by their reliance on fixed segment sizes, leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome this limitation, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel framework that dynamically adapts and tailors segments and their corresponding embedding weights for optimal retrieval accuracy. Comprising two interconnected components - a conventional transformer-based clip feature extractor and a token shifting and selection matcher - TS2-Net dynamically assesses and validates the relevance of tokens and features across different clips. By automating segment selection and adjusting weighting schemes during training, TS2-Net automates the process, eliminating the need for manual calculations. When evaluated on popular video question answering datasets, such as VQA-COCO and activity net, TS2-Net outperforms the current state-of-the-art approaches, establishing itself as a superior solution. The model's performance metrics and evaluation results can be viewed at: https://teaming.ai/content/text-clip-retrieval-dynamic-segment-selection-with-ts2-net. The main contribution of our work lies in the development of TS2-Net's token shifting and selection matcher module, which demonstrates its versatility by seamlessly integrating with current video transformer models for video question answering. It frames disturbance identification as a multi-label problem, treating each possible disturbance as an individual class. The proposed CNN leverages observation data at a single instant to generate a disturbance signature, which serves as the input for a fully connected network to compute probability values for each label. The framework's adaptability is demonstrated through its application to a wide range of coupling configurations and practical environments. It's worth noting that while this research explores multi-label disturbance identification, the theoretical framework is initially developed for single-label identification. By utilizing the self-consistent approach of $SU(N)$, $N=2$ mean-field theory, which accounts for the anisotropic spin-orbit coupling, we have observed a series of phase diagrams with various density wave patterns, including phase transitions between superfluid and density wave phases. Furthermore, the simulations show that the application of a synthetic magnetic field reveals a more complex pattern of phase transitions, including a re-entrant density wave phase, leading to a Smekal-Lawrence phase at low densities. Our study has also demonstrated that the critical temperatures of the cubic phase and other density wave states increase with the strength of the spin-orbit coupling. In the context of the $p$-wave mean-field model, we have identified an additional phase known as the diatomic phase, which exhibits an increased critical temperature with the strength of the spin-orbit coupling and the atomic hopping. Our study has further revealed a Smekal-Lawrence phase in $p$-wave mean-field model under a synthetic magnetic field, displaying similar characteristics to those observed in the $SU(2)$ mean-field model at low densities. A novel approach is introduced to create a vast array of Gaussian Process kernels utilizing fundamental mathematical expressions via symbolic algebra. Although discussing the symbolic expression of kernels offers insight into their characteristics, this article focuses on evaluating their practical utility in real-world applications. We examine approximately 6000 GP kernels generated through symbolic manipulation, demonstrating their effectiveness in handling 11 distinct datasets by employing Grid Search optimization of hyperparameters. Our results indicate that symbols GP kernels offer more options for improving prediction accuracy in comparison to traditional methods, thus potentially streamlining the hyperparameters optimization process in future research. We also discuss the significance of symbolic kernel compilation which significantly accelerates GPs training without compromising accuracy. Our proposed method can be accessed via online platforms or through self-hosting a local local copy which facilitates the reproduction of our experiments. By enhancing the repertoire of GP kernels and simplifying the training process, our approach makes GPs more accessible to researchers and practitioners. Additionally, we outline potential avenues for GP kernels expansion and training optimization. The primary contribution of this research is the systematic development of a large collection of GP kernels from basic mathematical expressions, which is accompanied by an open-source implementation. A local copy of the GP kernels library and a demonstration notebook of the GPs training process can be accessed via the provided GitHub links. The strategy development process for strategies beam-induced background reduction at future high-energy colliders has been shared, focusing on advancements in advanced materials and technological reduction methods. Software developers frequently collaborate on maintaining and updating existing code, including tests. Although test smells are recognized to have a negative impact on test code, there is a lack of in-depth understanding of their impact, particularly from the developer's viewpoint. To bridge this knowledge gap, a study delved into the developers' subjective views on the severity of five prominent test smells: (1) redundant tests, (2) tests lacking descriptive method names, (3) tests missing separate input validation, (4) tests including redundant input, and (5) tests verifying fixed input. A total of 504 developers participated in the study, which yielded 304 complete responses. To gauge the impact of these test smells, researchers used a scale of 1 to 11, similar to a previous study. Results indicated that developers consider redundant tests to be the most severe (2.73), followed by tests verifying fixed input (3.44), tests lacking descriptive method names (4.23), tests including redundant input (5.29), and finally, tests missing separate input validation with the least severity (6.23). A repeated-measures analysis revealed notable connections between developers' experience and the perceived severity of tests verifying fixed input and redundant tests. Additionally, descriptive analyses showed that a notable proportion of developers (14.6%) view none of the test smells as being particularly severe, while 4% believe all of these test smells are severe. These findings provide valuable insights for researchers, practitioners, and developers, offering a deeper understanding of the potential consequences of test smells, particularly from the perspective of the developers. To facilitate practical application of the study's results, researchers provided suggestions on how to effectively eliminate these test smells. These suggestions can be utilized as a starting point for refactoring test code, as well as guiding future studies on the topic. In many countries, (COVID-19) contact tracing operations have been established to track down individuals infected with the SARS-CoV-2 virus, aiming to contain the spread of the disease. As a result, the government of England launched the National Test and Trace Service, a large-scale COVID-19 contact tracing system, to assist in managing the outbreak. However, the system's efficiency has been compromised due to the limited capacity for contact tracing, which has led to the selection of a random subset of infected individuals, necessitating the need for local tracing partnerships to supplement the contact tracing system and enhance its performance. We developed a statistical model based on the binary match coefficient to compare the contact tracing efficiency of different local tracing partnerships. We discovered that the partnerships' effect on the contact tracing system's performance was time-dependent and that the longer the partnerships operate, the more notable the change in efficiency will be. Additionally, the binary match coefficient's behavior over time offers qualitative, easy-to-interpret indications of the contact tracing efficiency of the partnerships. Moreover, the model was used to assess the contact tracing efficiency of the Merseyside local tracing partnership, which showed that within seven days after the partnership's establishment, the National Test and Trace Service's contact tracing efficiency improved by 14% more than it would have without the partnership, which is a significant improvement of approximately 40% compared to the contact tracing efficiency of the Hampshire partnership. We discovered two key reasons for the variation in efficiency between the partnerships, which may be addressed by the National Test and Trace Service: first, the average age of the COVID-19 cases in the Merseyside partnership is younger than in the Hampshire partnership, which may have influenced the contact tracing efficiency, as younger individuals tend to have more active social networks and, therefore, a higher contact tracing efficiency; second, the Merseyside partnership appears to have formed close relationships with a higher proportion of their isolating contacts much faster than the Hampshire partnership. These findings imply that the contact tracing efficiency of the National Test and Trace Service is contingent on specific disease management factors, which the service has yet to consider. A significant challenge in computer vision research involves understanding 3D objects from 2D images. Although methods for reconstructing 3D objects exist, they often require step-by-step instruction and manual correction. An alternative strategy entails utilizing a robot arm assisted by a computer vision system that adjusts the position of a camera based on AI-generated instructions. Typically, training this system requires collecting and labeling vast numbers of data points, a time-consuming process that often proves impractical. To overcome these limitations, our study presents two innovative approaches that utilize a single image to calculate the necessary camera movements, using the image itself for self-correction. By testing these strategies with a simulated environment and a robotic setup, we found them to be both accurate and effective. In typical reinforcement learning, the agent's goals are autonomously discovered from high-level objectives through self-supervised exploration. By contrast, in the newly established field of reverse reinforcement learning (RRL), an external authority prescribes an agent's optimal behavior for a pre-defined set of situations, supplying the corresponding rewards in the process. This study investigates the multi-faceted complexities arising from the interplay between two fundamental aspects of RRL: 1) counterfactual explanations of how rewards influence decision-making and 2) the implications of imposing optimal behavioral constraints on the agent's parameter space. Both aspects yield profound implications in various domains, which are mirrored by the difficulties encountered in two complementary interpretations of RRL: 1) reverse learning to estimate a model's implicit reward function and 2) constrained planning to derive an optimal action strategy conditioned on specific assumptions regarding an unknown environment's properties. To resolve these challenges, this paper develops three mathematical frameworks: 1) the counterfactual regret experiment design, 2) the penalty complexity framework, and 3) the constrained MDP complexity. These theories ultimately enable the derivation of upper limits on the complexities resulting from RRL, which are then substantiated by illustrative examples and demonstrated in two practical applications, namely, 1) reverse RL-based autonomous driving and 2) personalized treatment optimization. These results imply that our findings have significant practical and theoretical significance for RRL. The presented theories represent a major advancement in the understanding of RRL and can be utilized to design more effective learning strategies. Moreover, this paper highlights important limitations of RRL that require further investigation. The temperature-dependent migration of polymers within a temperature gradient is examined in terms of the molecules' thermal expansion. A theoretical model of polymer chains possessing an internal flexible segment enables computation of their average segment orientation in response to thermal stimuli. The obtained results of polymer chain thermal response aligns synergistically with experimental data of cholesteric liquid crystals' helical twist in a temperature gradient, suggesting a common mechanism of thermal displacement governed by the anisotropic properties of internal flexible molecular segments. Moreover, the obtained results of polymer chain thermal response also coincide with experimental findings of polymers' thermal diffusion in a temperature gradient, indicating a significant role of internal molecular structures in the Soret effect. Theoretical models of thermal diffusion within a temperature gradient further confirm that internal molecular flexibility contributes substantially to the thermal diffusion process. Lastly, the magnitude of thermal motion within the polymer chains is found to be in alignment with the Soret coefficient, which signifies the distinct influence of molecular flexibility on the thermal migration of polymers within a temperature gradient. The theoretical models and methods employed in this study are broadly applicable to systems comprising molecular structures of variable length, suggesting their potential utility in the investigation of various micro-thermal phenomena. Furthermore, the obtained results of polymer chain thermal response also demonstrate a general relationship with the anisotropic properties of internal molecular segments, which is anticipated to hold true across a broad range of systems comprising molecular structures of variable size and influenced by external stimuli, including light. This study has thus implications for the understanding of various self-assembly processes and the molecular structure of the resulting materials across a wide range of conditions. Furthermore, the theoretical models and methods employed in this study have also identified a significant influence of the external stimuli on the thermal motion of the system, which is found to be in the form of an error function. technique combining the capabilities of transformer-language-model-based parsers

This research introduces a novel, unsupervised technique to significantly reduce false positives in domain adaptive pedestrian detection. Leveraging the structure of bounding boxes, our method accurately identifies valid pedestrian candidates, thereby minimizing errors. By incorporating a dynamic scoring system, our approach accurately measures the likelihood of object categories within a given box. To accommodate domain disparities, we utilize a robust object-distribution metric that ensures consistent object distributions across the two domains. Our method can be easily combined with existing domain adaptation approaches, including adaptive neural decoder (AND) and instance-weighting (IW) methods, resulting in the improved R$^2$AND and R-IW methods, which show substantial performance gains over the original AND and IW approaches, with a substantial 8.5 mAP improvement in the case of R-IW. Our fully unsupervised R$^2$AND method achieves a mAP rate of 57.2 on the Citypersons dataset, outperforming many state-of-the-art methods that employ annotated data from both domains. Our research demonstrates the utility of bounding box structure in domain adaptive object detection, thereby expanding the scope of unsupervised domain adaptation in this field. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel method utilizing a syntactic parser has been developed to generate phrasal parsing representations in parallel with NMT outputs during decoding.
The obtained phrasal parsing representations retain "mother-daughter" structural relationships, allowing for the incorporation of additional "mother" information as a enhanced decoding criterion, thus supplementing the standard NMT model with syntax-aware decoding. Experimental results on the English-to-German and English-to-Russian datasets of the WMT 2019 suggest that this approach leads to significant improvements in translation quality. Specifically, the model outperformed the NMT-only baseline by 3.19 BLEU points in the English-German direction and 2.85 BLEU points in the English-Russian direction. Furthermore, cross-lingual parsing evaluations demonstrated that the model's ability to accurately preserve tree structure exceeded that of the NMT-only baseline. Moreover, an analysis of parsing errors revealed that the model's performance could be elevated by increasing the quantity of samples during decoding, leading to a potential improvement of up to 1.5 BLEU points. The proposed method has been successfully applied to the task of syntax-guided machine translation, yielding superior results in the absence of any pre-existing alignment data. Accurate interpretations of spectroscopic and astronomical data rely heavily on the comprehensive databases that underpin them, and a novel development is the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, a database founded to support the astrochemical community. This platform bridges theory and observation by providing access to quantum mechanical calculations of binding energy distributions. Comprising 20 distinct species, BEAP features over 600 unique binding configurations, supplemented by experimental data and analysis, and serves as a resource for assessing the consistency between observations and theoretical frameworks. Furthermore, BEAP facilitates crucial comparisons with observational data, as demonstrated in a accompanying study involving millimeter-wave spectroscopy of hydrogen chloride. By fostering dialogue between theorists and astrochemists, BEAP aims to accelerate the integration of quantum mechanical theories into the field of astrochemistry. Obtaining further support, BEAP can expand its scope, potentially contributing to the evaluation of astrochemical models and playing a pivotal role in the interpretation of future high-resolution spectroscopic datasets. A demonstration of its functionality and recommended usage are provided in this work, and the platform is accessible at the website beap.science. Furthermore, the quantum mechanical input data and Python code underlying BEAP are available at the GitHub repository github.com/urth-pandemonium/beap.

Our circuits, derived from random Clifford gates, operate over an increasing number of qubits and layers in a controlled manner, allowing us to study the intricacy of quantum dynamics through their shadow formation process. By analyzing this structure, we can measure the level of unpredictability within the resulting expectation values. Notably, we've developed a practical, efficient framework for computing multi-qubit Traces, a technique that outperforms previous approaches by offering significantly lower depth and similar randomness. This breakthrough enables us to precisely gauge the depth required to achieve a specified level of error. Building on this insight, we've established tight approximation bounds for computing multi-qubit Traces using classical algorithms, thereby leveraging our Tracer framework to optimize the balance between circuit depth and computational overhead. These advancements have led to the creation of shallow-RRQ benchmarking suite that facilitates the efficient assessment of expectation values' depth requirements. Specifically, for various benchmark states, we've found the minimum average circuit depth needed to achieve a specified error threshold, and even reduced the practical minimum depth by nearly four orders of magnitude in some instances. Furthermore, we've discovered that the Tracer framework's efficiency plays a significant role in achieving these small error rates. Through an extensive investigation of quantum catalysis effects, we've tightened the gap between the Tracer framework's estimate and actual overlap for certain states, from around 25% to less than 5%. Our research includes comprehensive numerical analyses, supported by theoretical findings, that reveal the underlying principles governing the trade-off between circuit depth and assessment error rates. In the rapidly evolving field of meta-learning, particularly in reinforcement learning, various methods attempt to enable learning from limited experiences, with implications for expanding the capabilities of robotic systems. These methods typically employ pre-trained feature extractors or fixed feature manifolds, limiting the scope of meta-learning and hindering the development of more advanced systems. This work presents a groundbreaking approach to meta-learning, allowing a transformer-based model to discover and use complex, non-linear representations from raw image data, without the need for pre-trained foundations or rigid representation constraints. Our method has been effectively tested in the challenging task of transferring representations across diverse control tasks, demonstrating its ability to derive nuanced features and excel in subsequent learning applications. Additionally, its performance is comparable to those of methods utilizing pre-trained feature extractors, and it surpasses others on a range of meta-learning benchmarks. Moreover, the proposed model's ability to leverage its experiences and adjust its representations through self-supervision has been explored in a novel manner, showcasing a significant improvement in performance after a self-updating process. With the capacity for self-improvement in tandem with meta-learning, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art in complex control benchmarks. Despite operating in a supervised setting, our model's lack of prior knowledge from pre-trained datasets significantly limits its performance. Nevertheless, the proposed approach provides new avenues for meta-learning research and may form the basis of future innovations in reinforcement learning and robotic applications. The proposed model's source code has been made publicly available.

There is an ongoing contest in developing lightweight NMT models either by quantizing existing models or training smaller models through knowledge transfer. While quantization affects higher layer representations, knowledge distillation extracts information from both teacher model outputs and hidden states. Unlike quantization, knowledge distillation makes no hard assumptions about model architecture, but it's costly and assumes a comparable teacher model. In practice, knowledge distillation further accelerates model compression after quantization. This study examines the effects of using distillation in compressing NMT models from both fully trained and post-quantization state, exploring its interaction with different quantization methods and its impact on compression metrics. It reveals that distillation improves compression metrics, particularly when compressing smaller models, and significantly improves the stability of compression by mitigating variability and making it consistent with a chosen metric, regardless of the model state. Notably, its influence on the model's translation quality is minimal, and it does not enhance it. Distillation also prefers larger teacher and student model size, larger knowledge models, and higher learning rates, and it benefits from incorporating entropy reduction, especially when its loss outweighs the quantization loss. This study suggests that incorporating distillation in model compression can reduce the average compression metric variation by 60%. It provides quantitative measures of the effects of distillation on compression and model properties, and it identifies factors that make distillation easier to use, requiring no alterations to the training or inference code, and no additional computational overhead. These experiments guide the choice of development and compression strategies, and they indicate that distillation is easier to integrate than previously thought. In particular, it is easier to use in model state where quantization alone yields low compression metrics, and it is not necessary to rely solely on distillation in these cases. In model state where quantization fails, it is not necessary to use distillation consistently. The reliability of machine learning models for diagnostic purposes in medical imaging can be uncertain due to the potential for biased results if the model is not thoroughly tested for biases. For medical image analysis, obtaining complete annotation data can be impractical or even unfeasible, which necessitates the evaluation of alternate strategies. Our study explores the effectiveness of data augmentation methods in reducing the amount of labelled data needed for the precise detection of pneumonia within CT scans. Compared to a baseline model utilizing extensive labelled data, the proposed approach integrates data augmentation can achieve comparable results with a significantly reduced amount of labelled data, namely 10% of the original amount. Additionally, the proposed strategy exhibits robustness against unforeseen tests, demonstrating its practical value in real-world medical image analysis applications. We developed an automated method for identifying vertebrae in CT scans without manual input by utilizing the spine's longitudinal alignment. The approach involves detecting the vertebral bodies in a single slice, then rectifying adjacent slices to align with the original, resulting in a standardized spine anatomy. An optimization model, constrained by anatomical characteristics, uses predefined templates to identify the vertebrae. In this way, the method adapts to unique spinal shapes and configurations. Evaluations on three CT datasets, covering a range of anatomy types and imaging qualities, demonstrate robust performance with 98% accuracy, even in scans with artifacts or extreme pathology. Moreover, the method identifies individual vertebrae with 95% accuracy, and correctly aligns distorted spine sections, showcasing its flexibility and reliability. Notably, the method requires no user input, making it scalable to long scans, despite some loss of accuracy in severely distorted scans. The successful outcomes suggest that the technique could be applied to various automated spine segmentation tasks. We present detailed, step-by-step protocol on adapting our method to vertebral body CT scans, making it accessible without licensing restrictions. Furthermore, the source code is freely accessible and can be easily deployed on NVIDIA GPUs. The experimental results and visualizations provide valuable insights for medical imaging research, and the successful automation of vertebral identification and identification can be expanded to broader applications. Finally, the method has implications for further processing, such as automatic vertebral segmentation, tumor detection, and radiation therapy planning.
